reigns.tagline: The first doge, if he ever existed
reigns.previously: From 568, mainlanders flee the Lombards into the lagoon islands.
paragraphs: Venice started as a hiding place. From 568 the Lombards poured into northern Italy, and people from the mainland towns fled to the muddy islands of the lagoon, where horsemen couldn't follow. They fished, made salt and traded by boat. On paper they still belonged to the Byzantine Empire, ruled from distant Constantinople through its governor at Ravenna.

Venetian tradition says that in 697 the lagoon communities met at Heraclea and chose one leader for all of them: Paolo Lucio Anafesto. His title was dux, Latin for leader, which in Venetian speech became doge. The doge was elected, and he held the job for life. Nobody was ever born a doge.

Everything we know about him comes from chronicles written centuries later, by John the Deacon around 1000 and Doge Andrea Dandolo in the 1300s. He may have been a real lagoon chief, or a blurred memory of a Byzantine official. Either way Venice had its founding father, and the men who came after him were about to learn how dangerous the job could be.

claims.text: In 697 the lagoon communities gathered at Heraclea and elected Anafesto as their first doge.
claims.note: First told by John the Deacon around 1000, three centuries later. No document from the 690s mentions him.

claims.text: Anafesto is a garbled memory of the Byzantine exarch Paul of Ravenna.
claims.note: Some historians think the chroniclers turned the exarch Paul, in office in the 720s, into a local doge. Others accept a real lagoon leader behind the name.

claims.text: The title doge comes from the Latin dux.
claims.note: Dux was the title of Byzantine military commanders in Italy; doge is the Venetian form of the same word.

reigns.hook: Anafesto fades into legend. The chronicles name a second doge, Marcello Tegalliano, though he may really have been a Byzantine general with a borrowed title.

reigns.tagline: The second doge, or just a general with a good lawyer
reigns.previously: Anafesto, the first doge, fades into legend around 717.
paragraphs: The chronicles make Marcello Tegalliano the second doge, chosen at Heraclea after Anafesto. Then they run out of things to say. No deeds, no family, no death scene. For a man who supposedly ran the lagoon for nine years, he left almost no trace.

There is one real clue. More than a century later, a treaty between Venice and the Frankish emperor recalled that the border of Heraclea had been fixed with the Lombard king Liutprand in the days of a magister militum named Marcellus. So a Marcellus did command the lagoon's soldiers around this time. Whether anyone called him doge is another matter, and the next man to hold power would leave far less room for doubt.

claims.text: A magister militum named Marcellus fixed Heraclea's border with the Lombard king Liutprand.
claims.note: The Pactum Lotharii of 840 recalls the boundary agreed under Liutprand in Marcellus's time; most historians link him to the chronicles' Marcello.

claims.text: Marcello Tegalliano was the second doge of Venice.
claims.note: Only chronicles written centuries later call him doge. Many historians think he was a Byzantine military officer whom later Venetians promoted into their list of doges.

reigns.hook: Marcello fades out. In 726 the emperor in Constantinople bans holy images, and Italy boils over. The lagoon picks its own leader, Orso, the first doge historians are sure was real.

reigns.tagline: The first doge who was definitely real
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen in a revolt against the emperor
reigns.previously: Shadowy Marcello Tegalliano fades out around 726.
paragraphs: In 726 the Byzantine emperor Leo III ordered holy images destroyed. Italy was furious, and the Byzantine provinces there rose up and chose their own leaders instead of taking orders from Ravenna. The people of the lagoon met at Heraclea and chose Orso. He is the first doge whose existence historians accept.

Orso did not break with Constantinople for good. When the Lombards seized Ravenna, the seat of Byzantine Italy, the Venetian fleet helped win it back for the emperor's governor. The grateful emperor made Orso a hypatos, an honorary consul. The title stuck to the family as a surname: Ipato.
The real danger lay at home. Heraclea and its neighbour Jesolo hated each other, and in 737 that feud turned bloody. Orso was killed in the fighting. Venice had seen enough of doges for a while.

claims.text: Orso Ipato is the first doge whose existence is beyond doubt.
claims.note: Historians accept him as a real figure, though the stories about him come from later chronicles.

claims.text: The Venetian fleet helped the Byzantines win Ravenna back from the Lombards, and Orso got the title hypatos for it.
claims.note: The recapture is reported, but its date is unsure and some historians doubt the link between the battle and the title.

claims.text: Orso died in a feud between Heraclea and Jesolo.
claims.note: The chronicles agree he died violently in factional fighting in 737; the details come from much later writers.

reigns.hook: The doge is dead and the lagoon won't elect another. Instead it tries a new idea: a military governor who serves for just one year, then makes way for the next.

reigns.title: The Masters of the Soldiers
reigns.tagline: Five years, five governors, and a blinding at the end
reigns.relationToPredecessor: None; a new kind of office
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen for one year at a time
reigns.previously: Orso Ipato is killed in a feud and Venice gives up on doges.
paragraphs: After Orso Ipato was killed, the lagoon tried life without a doge. Power went instead to a magister militum, a master of the soldiers, the old Byzantine title for a local army commander. The twist was that each one served for just a year. Nobody would get the chance to dig in.

Five men held the post in turn: Domenico Leone, Felice Cornicola, Orso's son Teodato, Gioviano Ceparico and Giovanni Fabriciaco. Apart from their names and the order they came in, the chronicles tell us almost nothing. A year was too short to leave much of a mark.
The system didn't stop the violence. In 742 Giovanni Fabriciaco was overthrown and blinded. The lagoon decided that one leader for life, with all the risks that came with him, was better than this.

claims.text: For about five years the lagoon was run by military governors who each served a single year.
claims.note: The yearly rule comes from John the Deacon and later chronicles. Some historians think the governors were simply appointed from Ravenna.

claims.text: Giovanni Fabriciaco, the last of them, was deposed and blinded in 742.
claims.note: His blinding is recorded in the earliest Venetian chronicle and starts the run of blindings that follows.

reigns.hook: The experiment is over. The lagoon wants a doge again, and it picks a familiar name: Teodato Ipato, the murdered Orso's son, who has already done his year as governor.

reigns.tagline: The murdered doge's son comes back to the top
reigns.previously: The last yearly governor is blinded and Venice wants a doge again.
paragraphs: Teodato had already done a year as magister militum during the experiment with yearly governors. When it collapsed in 742, the lagoon went back to doges and chose him, the son of the murdered Orso. It was a sign the Ipato family still had friends.

Teodato moved the seat of government from Heraclea to Malamocco, on the long sand bar that shields the lagoon from the sea. Heraclea had been the scene of too many feuds. The world around him was shifting fast. In 751 the Lombards took Ravenna for good, and Byzantine rule in northern Italy was over in all but name.
Venice was now more on its own than ever. In 755 a rival named Galla Gaulo led a revolt. Teodato was seized, blinded and thrown out of office.

claims.text: Teodato moved the doge's seat from Heraclea to Malamocco.
claims.note: Reported by John the Deacon and accepted by most historians, though the move may have happened in stages.

claims.text: Teodato was blinded by his rival's followers.
claims.note: The blinding is in the earliest Venetian chronicle; blinding was the standard Byzantine way to disqualify a ruler.

reigns.hook: Teodato is blind and finished. The man behind the plot, Galla Gaulo, steps into the empty office. He is about to learn how short a doge's career can be.

reigns.tagline: He blinded the doge, then got the same treatment
reigns.previously: Teodato Ipato is overthrown, blinded and deposed.
paragraphs: Galla Gaulo got the job the violent way. He led the revolt that toppled Teodato Ipato in 755, and the lagoon accepted him as doge. The chronicles tell us almost nothing else about him, not even where he came from for sure.

He lasted about a year. In 756 his own enemies turned on him, and he got exactly what he had handed out: he was deposed, blinded and sent into exile. Two doges in a row had now lost their eyes. The Venetians decided their doges needed watching.

claims.text: Galla Gaulo was blinded and exiled after about a year.
claims.note: John the Deacon records his fall in his chronicle, and later lists agree on the short reign.

claims.text: Galla came from a Malamocco family and was also called Lupanio.
claims.note: The surname varies between chronicles, and his origins are not certain.

reigns.hook: Galla is gone. His successor, Domenico Monegario, gets the job with a catch: two tribunes elected every year will sit beside him and check everything he does.

reigns.tagline: A doge with minders, and still he lost his eyes
reigns.cameToPower: Elected, with two tribunes to watch him
reigns.previously: Galla Gaulo is blinded and exiled after a year as doge.
paragraphs: Domenico Monegario came from Malamocco, now the seat of government. The lagoon gave him the top job but tied his hands. Two tribunes were elected each year to sit beside him, a first attempt to stop a doge acting like a king.

It didn't save him. Outside the lagoon, the Frankish king Pepin the Short was crushing the Lombards on the pope's behalf, and the old balance of power in Italy was breaking. Inside it, the factions of Heraclea and Malamocco kept fighting. In 764 Monegario was deposed and blinded, the third doge in a row to lose his eyes.

claims.text: Two tribunes were elected each year to keep watch on the doge.
claims.note: Reported by John the Deacon; historians debate how much real power the tribunes had.

claims.text: Monegario was the third doge running to be deposed and blinded.
claims.note: The earliest Venetian chronicle records the blinding of Teodato, Galla and Monegario in turn.

reigns.hook: Three blinded doges in a row. Next the lagoon turns to Maurizio Galbaio of Heraclea, a man who wants something new: to keep the office in his own family.

reigns.tagline: Twenty years in office and he kept his eyes
reigns.previously: Domenico Monegario is deposed and blinded in 764.
paragraphs: After three blindings, Maurizio Galbaio brought some calm. He came from an old Heraclea family, which later claimed descent from the Roman emperor Galba. In 774 the Franks under Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom, so Venice now had a powerful new neighbour on the mainland, and Maurizio kept on good terms with Byzantium.

He had a plan for after his death. In 778 he made his son Giovanni co-doge, the first attempt to turn the office into a family business. A bishopric was also set up on the island of Olivolo, the future cathedral of Venice. In 787 Maurizio died in his bed, still in office, the first doge in a long time who wasn't forced out.

claims.text: The Galbaio family descended from the Roman emperor Galba.
claims.note: A flattering family tradition; there is no evidence at all.

claims.text: The bishopric of Olivolo, later the see of Venice, was founded in Maurizio's reign.
claims.note: Usually dated around 775, but the founding date is uncertain.

claims.text: Maurizio made his son co-doge in 778.
claims.note: Recorded by John the Deacon, and it set a pattern later doges copied.

reigns.hook: The old doge dies peacefully, and his son Giovanni simply carries on. The Galbaio dynasty seems to have worked. Then Giovanni picks a fight with the Church.

reigns.tagline: Father to son to grandson, and then the tower
reigns.previously: Old Maurizio Galbaio dies in office after more than twenty years.
paragraphs: Giovanni Galbaio had been co-doge for nine years when his father died, so he simply took over. In 796 he made his own son Maurizio co-doge too. Three generations of one family: it looked very like a royal house.

The Galbaii backed Byzantium, but plenty of Venetians wanted closer ties with Charlemagne's Franks, and the Patriarch of Grado was one of them. In 802 the younger Maurizio sailed to Grado and took the patriarch prisoner. According to the chronicles he was thrown from the top of a tower.

That killing turned the lagoon against them. The dead patriarch's nephew Fortunatus took his place and stirred up the pro-Frankish party. Around 803 or 804 father and son fled to Mantua and disappear from the story.

claims.text: In 802 the Patriarch of Grado was thrown to his death from a tower.
claims.note: Told by John the Deacon two centuries later. The patriarch's violent death is accepted; the tower can't be checked.

claims.text: Giovanni Galbaio made his son Maurizio co-doge in 796.
claims.note: Recorded in the earliest Venetian chronicle.

reigns.hook: The Galbaii have run for the mainland. The pro-Frankish party has won, and its leader, a Malamocco tribune named Obelerio, is about to bet Venice's future on Charlemagne.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; led the rival party
reigns.reignEnded: Blamed for the war and exiled, 811
reigns.previously: The Galbaio doges flee to Mantua after the patriarch's murder.
paragraphs: Obelerio was a tribune from Malamocco and the leader of the party that favoured the Franks. He ruled alongside his brother Beato as co-doge. At Christmas 805 the two of them turned up at Charlemagne's court at Thionville with gifts, and the Frankish emperor set about organising Venice's affairs. Byzantium was not amused.

A Byzantine fleet sailed into the Adriatic, and Obelerio switched sides. That annoyed the Franks. In 810 Charlemagne's son Pepin, king of Italy, attacked the lagoon. The Venetians pulled back to the islands of Rialto, deep in the lagoon where Pepin's ships couldn't reach them. Pepin withdrew and died that summer.
Someone had to take the blame, and in 811 Obelerio was driven out. Years later, around 831, he tried to come back and was killed. His head was put on show in the market.

claims.text: Obelerio and Beato visited Charlemagne at Thionville at Christmas 805.
claims.note: The Royal Frankish Annals record the visit of the two dukes of Venice with gifts.

claims.text: The Venetians lured Pepin's fleet onto the shallows and beat him.
claims.note: Venetian chronicles tell a heroic victory. The Frankish royal annals say Pepin forced Venice to submit before he fell ill and died that year.

claims.text: Obelerio was killed trying to return around 831, and his head was displayed in the market.
claims.note: Told by John the Deacon; the date of the attempt varies.

reigns.hook: Obelerio is gone, and the Venetians who held out at Rialto decide to stay there. The new doge, Agnello Partecipazio, will build his palace on the islands. A city is about to be born.

reigns.tagline: The doge who moved to Rialto and started Venice
reigns.previously: Pepin's attack fails and Doge Obelerio is driven out.
paragraphs: Agnello Partecipazio was a Heraclea noble who had held out at Rialto during Pepin's attack. As doge he moved the government there for good. Rialto was a cluster of islands in the middle of the lagoon, hard to reach for any army. He built a ducal palace on the spot where the Doge's Palace stands today. The city of Venice proper begins here.

Peace helped. Between 812 and 814 the Franks and the Byzantines agreed that the lagoon would stay Byzantine, so Venice could trade with both. Agnello still wanted the office to stay in the family. He made his son Giustiniano co-doge, then his younger son Giovanni too, and the brothers fell out. When Agnello died in 827, Giustiniano took over.

claims.text: Agnello built the first ducal palace where the Doge's Palace now stands.
claims.note: Venetian chronicles say so, and the site has been the seat of government ever since.

claims.text: Agnello had defended Rialto during Pepin's attack of 810.
claims.note: A Venetian tradition that explains his election; there is no contemporary record of his part in the fighting.

reigns.hook: Agnello's son Giustiniano inherits a new city with an old problem: it has no famous saint. Two merchants in Egypt are about to fix that with the boldest theft in Venetian history.

reigns.tagline: The doge who got a stolen saint
reigns.previously: Agnello Partecipazio, founder of Rialto's palace, dies in 827.
paragraphs: Giustiniano had been co-doge for years, so when his father died he stepped up. His reign lasted barely two years, but one event in it changed Venice forever.

In 828 two Venetian merchants, Buono of Malamocco and Rustico of Torcello, took the body of St Mark the Evangelist from its church in Alexandria and shipped it home. The story goes that they hid it under pork so Muslim customs men wouldn't look. Venice now owned an apostle, and the winged lion of St Mark became its badge.
Giustiniano left money in his will for a chapel for the saint beside the palace, the first St Mark's. Before he died in 829 he called back his exiled brother Giovanni to share power.

claims.text: The merchants hid St Mark's body under pork to get it past Muslim customs.
claims.note: It comes from the Venetian account of the theft, written to glorify the city, and was later shown in the mosaics of St Mark's.

claims.text: Giustiniano's will paid for the first church of St Mark beside the palace.
claims.note: His will survives in a later copy and is accepted by historians.

claims.text: The body brought to Venice really was St Mark's.
claims.note: Nobody can prove it either way. One modern theory claims the bones are Alexander the Great's, which most historians dismiss.

reigns.hook: Giustiniano dies with the saint's chapel still being built. His brother Giovanni, called home from exile, now rules alone. Not everyone in the lagoon is happy about it.

reigns.tagline: Thrown out twice, the second time into a monastery
reigns.previously: Giustiniano Partecipazio dies, and St Mark has a home in Venice.
paragraphs: Giovanni had been exiled after quarrelling with his brother, then brought back to share the office. Once alone, he had enemies everywhere. Around 831 old Obelerio tried a comeback from his base at Malamocco. Giovanni crushed him, burned the rebels' settlements and had his head put on show.

Then a tribune named Caroso seized the palace, and Giovanni had to flee to the Frankish court. Caroso's rule lasted only months before he was overthrown and blinded, and Giovanni came back. But in 836 his enemies grabbed him at church, shaved his head like a monk's and shipped him off to Grado. He died there the next year.

claims.text: A tribune named Caroso briefly took power while Giovanni was away.
claims.note: Reported by John the Deacon; the exact dates, around 832, are uncertain.

claims.text: In 836 Giovanni was seized at church, tonsured and sent to Grado.
claims.note: Recorded by John the Deacon, the nearest chronicle to the event.

reigns.hook: Giovanni is a monk in Grado. The lagoon chooses Pietro Tradonico, a rough soldier who, it is said, can't even sign his own name. He will rule for nearly thirty years.

reigns.tagline: Twenty-eight years as doge, then knives after vespers
reigns.previously: Giovanni I Partecipazio is seized at church and shaved as a monk.
paragraphs: Pietro Tradonico took over in 836, after rivals bundled Giovanni I Partecipazio off to a monastery. He quickly made his son Giovanni co-doge, the standard move by now. Venetian tradition says the new doge couldn't even write his own name. He turned out to be one of the toughest operators the lagoon had seen.

In 840 he made the first written pact between Venice and the Frankish emperors, with Lothar I. It fixed the borders and let Venetian merchants trade on the mainland. At sea he had less luck. Venice sent ships to help the Byzantines against Arab raiders in southern Italy, and around 840 they were wiped out near Taranto. Slav pirates from the Narenta river on the Dalmatian coast kept raiding too.

His son and co-doge died before him, leaving the old man exposed. On 13 September 864, as he came out of vespers at the convent church of San Zaccaria, a band of conspirators from leading families fell on him and killed him. Twenty-eight years in charge ended on the church steps.

claims.text: Pietro Tradonico could not write and signed documents with a mark.
claims.note: The story comes from later Venetian chronicles and can't be checked against his own documents with any certainty.

claims.text: In 840 he agreed the Pactum Lotharii with the emperor Lothar I.
claims.note: The text survives in later copies, and later emperors renewed it again and again.

claims.text: He was murdered by conspirators at San Zaccaria in 864.
claims.note: Recorded by John the Deacon, the nearest chronicle to the event.

reigns.hook: The old doge lies dead outside the church. Venice turns to Orso Partecipazio, and his first job is to hunt down the killers.

paragraphs: Orso Partecipazio started by settling the score. The men who had killed Pietro Tradonico were tracked down and punished, some with death and others with exile. The message was plain: murdering a doge would no longer pay. Orso came from the Partecipazio clan, the family that had given Venice its first doges at Rialto, and he meant to keep the office in their hands.

Outside the lagoon he had fighting to do. Arab raiders were probing the Adriatic and Slav pirates from the Dalmatian coast never let up, and Venetian fleets went out against both. He stayed close to Constantinople too, and the chronicles say he sent the emperor Basil I a present of twelve great bells.

Orso made his son Giovanni co-doge, so when he died in 881 the job passed straight to the next Partecipazio. Venice still elected its doges, on paper. In practice one family kept handing the office down.

claims.text: Orso sent twelve great bells to the emperor Basil I in Constantinople.
claims.note: Told by John the Deacon about a century later; no Byzantine writer mentions the gift.

claims.text: Orso belonged to the same family as the first Rialto doges, Agnello and Giustiniano.
claims.note: The chronicles call them all Partecipazio, but the family links between the 9th-century doges are not proven.

reigns.tagline: A sick doge who gave up the job, then had to come back
reigns.previously: Orso I Partecipazio dies, and his co-doge son takes over.
paragraphs: Giovanni II had already been his father's co-doge, so the handover in 881 was smooth. His big target was Comacchio, a town in the Po delta that competed with Venice for salt and river trade. The chronicles say his brother Badoario went to Rome to ask the pope for it, was ambushed by the local count on the way home and died of his wounds. Giovanni answered by seizing the town.

Then his health gave way. In 887 he stepped down in favour of Pietro Candiano, the first doge of a family that would dominate the next century. When Candiano was killed only months later, the ailing Giovanni had to come back as caretaker until a new doge could be chosen. He died soon after, in 887 or 888.

claims.text: His brother Badoario died after an ambush by the count of Comacchio, and Giovanni took the town in revenge.
claims.note: The story is in John the Deacon; who attacked whom, and why, is unclear.

claims.text: Giovanni returned as caretaker doge after Pietro I Candiano's death in 887.
claims.note: Recorded by John the Deacon; he held on only until Pietro Tribuno was elected.

paragraphs: Pietro Candiano was elected in the spring of 887, when the ailing Giovanni II gave up the office. He was the first doge of the Candiano family, which would supply four more over the next ninety years. He wanted to make his mark fast, and the obvious enemy was the Narentines, Slav pirates from around the mouth of the Narenta river in Dalmatia who preyed on Venetian ships.

He sailed down the Adriatic at the head of a war fleet. On 18 September 887 his ships met the pirates in battle off the Dalmatian coast, and the doge was killed in the fighting, about five months after his election. Venice was left without a doge, and old, sick Giovanni II had to come back to keep the seat warm.

claims.text: Pietro I Candiano was killed in battle with the Narentines on 18 September 887.
claims.note: John the Deacon gives the battle and the date.

reigns.tagline: He walled the city just in time for the Magyars
reigns.previously: Pietro I Candiano is killed fighting pirates after five months.
paragraphs: Pietro Tribuno took over in 888 after Giovanni II's brief second spell, and he lasted 24 years. The chronicles make him a grandson of Pietro Tradonico. His big idea was defence. He built a wall running from the Castello end of the city to Santa Maria Zobenigo, and a chain could be stretched across the Grand Canal to stop enemy ships.

The danger was real. The Magyars, horsemen from the Hungarian plain, had poured into northern Italy, and in 899 they pushed into the lagoon, burning outlying settlements. In 900 the Venetian fleet met them at Albiola, at the edge of the lagoon, and beat them. They never came back.
Behind the new wall the city filled in. Rialto was turning from a cluster of islands into a real town, and when Pietro Tribuno died in 912 he left it far safer than he found it.

claims.text: The Venetians beat the Magyars at Albiola in 900.
claims.note: Recorded by John the Deacon, writing about a century later.

claims.text: A chain could be drawn across the Grand Canal as part of his defences.
claims.note: Described by John the Deacon and Andrea Dandolo; no trace of the wall or chain survives.

claims.text: Pietro Tribuno was a grandson of Pietro Tradonico.
claims.note: The chronicles say so, but early Venetian family trees are patchy.

reigns.tagline: Twenty peaceful years, then off to a monastery
reigns.previously: Pietro Tribuno dies after walling the city and beating the Magyars.
paragraphs: After the Magyar scare, Venice wanted calm, and Orso II Partecipazio gave it twenty years of it. He stayed on good terms with Constantinople, which made him a protospatharios, a high court rank, and with the kings who fought over northern Italy. Venetian merchants kept moving goods between the two worlds, and for once nobody burned anything.

Family drama filled the gap. Early in his reign his son Pietro was sailing home from Constantinople when a Slav prince on the Dalmatian coast seized him and handed him over to Simeon, the ruler of Bulgaria. Venice had to bargain to get him back.
In 932 Orso gave up the office of his own free will and retired to a monastery in the lagoon, where he died. Few doges managed such a quiet exit.

claims.text: Orso II stepped down freely and became a monk.

reigns.tagline: He burned a rival town and starved out another
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; son of Pietro I Candiano
reigns.previously: Orso II Partecipazio retires to a monastery after twenty quiet years.
paragraphs: Pietro II Candiano was the son of the doge the Narentines had killed, and he was about 60 when he was elected in 932. He was in a hurry. That same year Venetian forces fell on Comacchio, the salt town in the Po delta that kept competing with Venice, and destroyed it. Comacchio never challenged Venice again.

Then he turned on Istria. When the marquis of Istria and his towns seized Venetian goods, the doge didn't send a fleet. He banned all trade with them. Before long Capodistria and the other Istrian towns came asking for terms, promising to protect Venetian merchants. It was an early sign of how Venice liked to win: by squeezing the purse.
He died in 939, with Venice now plainly the leading power of the northern Adriatic.

claims.text: A trade embargo forced the Istrian towns and their marquis to make peace on Venice's terms.

paragraphs: Pietro Partecipazio, also known by the later family name Badoer, was the son of Orso II. As a young man he had been sent to Constantinople and honoured at the emperor's court, only to be seized on the way home and handed over to the Bulgarians. Venice got him back, and about a quarter of a century later it made him doge.

His reign was short and quiet, three years squeezed between two Candiano doges. The chronicles record almost nothing about it: no wars, no plots, no fires. He died in 942, and the Candiano family came straight back.

claims.text: On his way home from Constantinople he was captured by the prince of Zahumlje and sent to Simeon of Bulgaria.

claims.text: The Partecipazio family later took the name Badoer.
claims.note: Venetian tradition links the Badoer to the Partecipazio doges; the line of descent can't be traced with certainty.

reigns.tagline: Kidnapped brides, and a son who turned pirate
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; son of Pietro II Candiano
reigns.previously: Pietro Partecipazio dies after three quiet years as doge.
paragraphs: Pietro III Candiano, son of Pietro II, sent fleets against the Narentine pirates, but Venice remembered his reign for a better story. Brides gathered at San Pietro di Castello for a group wedding were snatched by pirates. The men of the city chased them down, killed the kidnappers and brought every bride home. The Feast of the Marys celebrated it for centuries.

The real trouble was at home. He made his son, another Pietro, co-doge, and the young man rebelled against him. The revolt failed. The son was spared at his father's plea, but exiled, and the Venetians swore never to accept him as doge. He went to the mainland, gathered ships and turned pirate, preying on Venetian merchants around the river mouths near Ravenna.
The old doge died in 959, said to be heartbroken. Soon afterwards Venice forgot its oath and sent ships to bring the pirate son home as doge.

claims.text: Pirates kidnapped Venetian brides and the city's men rescued them, the origin of the Feast of the Marys.
claims.note: The tale comes from later chronicles, which usually set it in his reign. The festival itself was real and was dropped in the late 1300s.

claims.text: The Venetians swore never to accept the rebel son as doge, then elected him anyway.
claims.note: John the Deacon records the exile and the son's election in 959.

claims.text: Pietro III died of grief over his son's rebellion.
claims.note: A chronicler's moral, not a medical record.

reigns.tagline: He acted like a prince, and Venice burned him out
reigns.previously: Pietro III Candiano dies, and Venice recalls his exiled son.
paragraphs: The exiled pirate came home in style, fetched by a fleet of Venetian ships. Pietro IV Candiano started well: a law of 960 banned Venetians from the slave trade. Then he sent his wife Giovanna into the convent of San Zaccaria, steered their son Vitale into the Church, and married Waldrada, sister of the marquis of Tuscany, who brought him huge estates on the mainland.

Now he lived like a mainland lord. He hired foreign soldiers as guards, dragged Venice into his wife's quarrels on the mainland and stayed close to the German emperor Otto I. Plenty of Venetians saw a would-be king. In August 976 a crowd stormed the palace. When the guards held them off, someone set fire to the houses next door. The palace went up, and the flames spread to St Mark's.

Pietro tried to escape through the atrium of St Mark's with his baby son. The crowd caught them and killed them both, and their bodies were thrown out at the butchers' market before someone took them away for burial. His son Vitale, the churchman, fled to the German court to plot revenge.

claims.text: Pietro IV and his infant son were killed by the mob as they fled the burning palace.
claims.note: John the Deacon, writing within a generation, records both killings.

claims.text: The bodies were dumped at the butchers' market before being taken away for burial.
claims.note: Told by John the Deacon and later chroniclers; the details of who rescued the bodies vary.

claims.text: A law of 960 under Pietro IV banned Venetians from trading in slaves.
claims.note: The decree survives. How well it was enforced is another matter.

reigns.hook: The palace is ash and St Mark's has burned. Venice needs someone calm, rich and pious to clean up. It picks a noble named Pietro Orseolo.

reigns.tagline: The doge who slipped out one night and became a monk
reigns.reignEnded: Fled at night to a monastery
reigns.previously: Pietro IV Candiano is cut down fleeing his burning palace.
paragraphs: Pietro Orseolo took over a smoking city. He was rich and deeply religious, and the chronicles say he dug into his own fortune to rebuild the ducal palace and the church of St Mark. For two years he worked to calm a city that had just murdered its last doge.

Then, one night in September 978, he vanished. Without a word to his wife or son, he slipped out of Venice with a few companions, among them the abbot of Cuxa and the hermit Romuald, and made for the abbey of Saint-Michel-de-Cuxa in the Pyrenees. He spent the rest of his life there as a monk, and the Church later made him a saint.
Venice was left without a doge, and his family without a husband and father. But the Orseoli weren't finished. His son, also called Pietro, would become the greatest doge Venice had yet seen.

claims.text: He paid for rebuilding the palace and St Mark's out of his own pocket.
claims.note: John the Deacon and later Andrea Dandolo praise his generosity; how much came from his own fortune can't be checked.

claims.text: He left Venice secretly at night, without telling his family.
claims.note: John the Deacon, writing within living memory, and Peter Damian's life of St Romuald both describe the secret flight.

claims.text: Pietro Orseolo is a saint.
claims.note: Venerated soon after his death; his cult was formally approved by the papacy in 1731.

reigns.hook: Venice wakes to find its doge gone. Oddly, it turns to the family it burned out two years before and elects Vitale Candiano, brother of the murdered doge.

paragraphs: When Pietro Orseolo vanished to a monastery in the Pyrenees, Venice did something surprising. It elected Vitale Candiano, brother of the doge the mob had murdered two years earlier. The choice was about peace. Pietro IV's son, the patriarch Vitale, had run to the German emperor Otto II, and the angry Candiani and their German friends were a real danger to the city.

The new doge set about calming things down and mending fences with Otto II. But he fell ill after about fourteen months. In 979 he gave up the office and retired to a monastery, where he died soon after.

reigns.tagline: A weak doge, a family feud and a German blockade
reigns.previously: Vitale Candiano falls ill and retires to a monastery.
paragraphs: Tribuno Memmo was rich and well connected, and his best-remembered act was a gift. In 982 he handed the island of San Giorgio Maggiore to the Benedictine monk Giovanni Morosini to found a monastery. Monks lived there for over eight centuries, and Palladio's church still stands on the island.

Keeping order was another matter. Two clans, the Caloprini and the Morosini, fell into a deadly feud, and the doge couldn't control it. After a Morosini was murdered, the Caloprini fled to the German emperor Otto II and offered to help him take Venice. In 983 Otto blockaded the lagoon, cutting the city off from mainland trade. Venice was saved by luck: Otto died at the end of that year and the blockade collapsed.

The feud rumbled on, and Memmo looked weaker every year. In 991 he was pushed out of office and into a monastery, where he died soon after. Venice wanted a strong hand again, and it knew which family to ask.

claims.text: Otto II blockaded Venice in 983 at the urging of the exiled Caloprini.

reigns.tagline: The doge who sailed out and made the Adriatic Venetian
reigns.previously: Tribuno Memmo is eased out of office and into a monastery.
paragraphs: Pietro II Orseolo thought big. In 992 he won a golden bull from the Byzantine emperor Basil II that cut the duties Venetian ships paid at Constantinople, and he made friends with the German emperors too. Venice was learning to play the two great empires off against each other.

On Ascension Day in the year 1000 he set sail with a war fleet to deal with the Narentine pirates who preyed on Adriatic shipping. Town after town on the Dalmatian coast submitted, and he took the title Duke of the Dalmatians. Venice marked the day with a blessing of the sea, the seed of its later Marriage of the Sea.

In 1001 the young emperor Otto III slipped into Venice in secret to visit him. The doge's son Giovanni married a Byzantine princess, Maria, but plague killed them both a few years later. Pietro died in 1009, and his younger son Otto stepped into his place.

claims.text: Maria, the Byzantine bride, shocked Venice by eating with a little golden fork.

claims.text: The Ascension Day ceremony of the sea began with the expedition of 1000.
claims.note: Venetian tradition links the two. The ring dropped into the water belongs to a later story, set in 1177.

reigns.tagline: A teenage doge with a king for a brother-in-law
reigns.previously: Pietro II Orseolo dies, and his teenage son Otto takes over.
paragraphs: Otto Orseolo was named after his godfather, the emperor Otto III, and became doge at about 16. His family looked unstoppable. His wife was a sister of King Stephen I of Hungary. One brother, Orso, was Patriarch of Grado, and another, Vitale, was Bishop of Torcello. To plenty of Venetians this looked less like a republic and more like a royal house in the making.

Trouble came from Poppo, Patriarch of Aquileia, who wanted Grado for himself. In the early 1020s Otto and Orso were chased out of Venice by their enemies, then called back when things went badly without them. The peace didn't last. In 1026 Otto was overthrown for good. His beard was shaved off as a mark of disgrace and he was shipped off to Constantinople.
He never came home, and died in exile around 1032. His son Peter did better abroad. When King Stephen died in 1038, Peter Orseolo, the Venetian nephew, became King of Hungary.

claims.text: Otto's beard was shaved off before he was sent into exile.
claims.note: Told by later Venetian chroniclers such as Andrea Dandolo. Shaving was a familiar way to humiliate a fallen ruler, but no account from the time survives.

claims.text: Otto's wife was a sister of King Stephen I of Hungary.
claims.note: Their son Peter's claim to the Hungarian throne rested on it. Her own name is not known for certain.

claims.text: Otto's son Peter Orseolo became King of Hungary.
claims.note: Peter succeeded Stephen in 1038, was driven out in 1041 and ruled again from 1044 to 1046.

reigns.tagline: The anti-Orseolo doge nobody abroad would back
reigns.reignEnded: Forced out and made a monk
reigns.previously: Otto Orseolo is deposed, shaved and shipped off to Constantinople.
paragraphs: Pietro Barbolano, also called Centranico, was the choice of the families who had thrown out the Orseoli. Now Venice had to live with what it had done. The Byzantine court had liked the Orseoli, and the German emperor Conrad II saw no reason to help a doge put in by a revolt.

Conrad sided with Poppo of Aquileia, who was still after Grado, and Barbolano could do little to stop him. With no friends abroad and the Orseolo party strong at home, his support fell away. Around 1030 he was pushed out, made to take a monk's vows and sent to Constantinople, down the same road Otto had taken.

claims.text: Barbolano and Centranico are two names for the same doge.
claims.note: The chronicles use one name or the other, or both. Modern lists of doges give both.

claims.text: Barbolano was forced to become a monk and sent to Constantinople.
claims.note: This is Andrea Dandolo's account, written over 300 years later. Even the year he fell, 1030 or 1032, is uncertain.

reigns.hook: With Barbolano gone, the Orseoli make one last grab. When it fails, a Venice sick of the whole clan turns to a silk merchant, Domenico Flabanico.

reigns.tagline: The silk merchant who banned dynasties
reigns.previously: Pietro Barbolano is made a monk and sent away to Constantinople.
paragraphs: After Barbolano's fall the Orseoli tried once more. Patriarch Orso ran the city for his exiled brother Otto, but Otto died in Constantinople. Then another Orseolo, Domenico, seized the palace and lasted a single day before he fled. Venice had had enough. In 1032 it chose Domenico Flabanico, a rich silk merchant from a family that had never produced a doge.

Flabanico made sure no family could take over again. A new law banned any doge from naming a co-doge or an heir, and the Orseoli were barred from office. Councillors were set beside the doge to share his decisions. Then he ruled quietly for about eleven years and died in office. It was a dull reign, and that was the point.

claims.text: Flabanico's law banned doges from naming co-doges or heirs.
claims.note: Recorded by Andrea Dandolo and accepted by historians as the end of the ducal dynasties.

claims.text: Councillors were first set beside the doge in his time.
claims.note: The chroniclers credit Flabanico, but documents show the ducal councillors clearly only later, in the 12th century.

claims.text: Domenico Orseolo held the palace for just one day.
claims.note: The story comes from Andrea Dandolo's chronicle. It is neat enough to make some historians wary.

reigns.hook: Flabanico dies with the doge's powers clipped. The next doge, Domenico Contarini, will rule for almost 30 years and start the golden church of St Mark that still stands.

reigns.tagline: He began the St Mark's you can still visit
reigns.previously: Domenico Flabanico dies, and doges can no longer name their heirs.
paragraphs: Domenico Contarini was the first doge from a family that would give Venice eight of them. His long reign was mostly calm. He mended relations with the German emperors and kept the trade with Byzantium flowing. When Zara, the key port on the Dalmatian coast, slipped out of Venice's grip, he brought it back into line.

His great project was a church. The old St Mark's, patched up after the fire of 976, was too small and too plain for a city that was getting rich. In 1063 work began on a new basilica, built to the plan of the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople. It is the domed church that still stands on the Piazza. Contarini didn't live to see it finished. He died in 1071.

claims.text: The new St Mark's copied the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople.
claims.note: Historians agree on the model. The Holy Apostles was pulled down after 1453, so St Mark's is the best guide to what it looked like.

claims.text: Contarini won Zara back around 1050.
claims.note: The chroniclers are vague, and the year and details are uncertain.

reigns.hook: Contarini dies. Outside San Nicolò on the Lido, a crowd in boats starts chanting one name before anyone has counted a vote: Domenico Selvo.

reigns.tagline: A Byzantine bride, a golden bull and a lost battle
reigns.cameToPower: Acclaimed by a crowd in boats
reigns.previously: Domenico Contarini dies after starting the new St Mark's.
paragraphs: Selvo's election is the first we have from an eyewitness. A priest, Domenico Tino, saw a huge crowd in boats outside San Nicolò al Lido shouting that they wanted Domenico Selvo. The new doge was rowed to St Mark's, walked in barefoot and took his staff of office from the altar. He married Theodora, a Byzantine princess, tying Venice even closer to Constantinople.

That tie paid off. In 1081 the Normans of southern Italy under Robert Guiscard invaded the Byzantine Balkans, and Emperor Alexios I begged Venice for ships. A Venetian fleet beat the Normans off Durazzo. The reward was a golden bull that let Venetian merchants trade across the empire without paying duties and gave them their own quarter in Constantinople.
Then the luck ran out. In 1084 the Normans smashed the Venetian fleet off Corfu. Back home Selvo took the blame and was deposed. He spent his last years as a monk and died in 1087.

claims.text: Selvo's Greek wife scandalised Venice with her golden fork and her perfumes.
claims.note: The churchman Peter Damian told a preachy tale about a pampered Greek wife of a doge. Some versions pin it on Theodora, others on Maria, the wife of Giovanni Orseolo.

claims.text: Theodora was a sister of Emperor Michael VII Doukas.
claims.note: Venetian sources say so, but her exact place in the Doukas family is uncertain.

claims.text: Alexios I's golden bull for Venice dates from 1082.
claims.note: Most historians accept 1082. Some argue for 1092, in a later doge's reign. It survives only in later copies.

reigns.hook: Selvo is gone, but Venice keeps the golden bull. His successor, Vitale Faliero, gets to spend the profits, and to finish the basilica.

reigns.tagline: He got the profits, and a miracle in St Mark's
reigns.previously: Domenico Selvo loses to the Normans off Corfu and is deposed.
paragraphs: Vitale Faliero took over a Venice that was getting rich fast. The Byzantine trade deal was paying off, and the Norman threat faded when Robert Guiscard died in 1085. Faliero stayed close to Constantinople, and Venetian merchants spread through the empire's ports.

His reign is remembered for St Mark's. The new basilica was ready to be consecrated in 1094, but there was a snag: nobody knew where the saint's body was. It had been hidden during the rebuilding, and the secret had died with the men who knew it. Venice fasted and prayed for three days. Then, the story goes, a pillar cracked open to reveal the body. Faliero died soon afterwards, around 1095.

claims.text: St Mark's body reappeared from a pillar after three days of prayer.
claims.note: The miracle is shown in a 13th-century mosaic inside St Mark's. It's a pious story, not a record.

claims.text: The new St Mark's was consecrated in 1094.
claims.note: The date comes from Venetian tradition and is widely accepted. Work on the decoration went on for centuries.

reigns.hook: Faliero dies with the basilica open. In the East, the pope's crusade is under way, and Venice's rivals Pisa and Genoa are already sailing. The next doge, Vitale Michiel, has to decide whether to join them.

reigns.tagline: Late to the crusade, and fighting Pisa first
reigns.previously: Vitale Faliero dies after St Mark's body miraculously reappears.
paragraphs: Vitale Michiel took office as the First Crusade was being preached. Venice held back at first, since war with the Muslim powers was bad for trade. But Pisa and Genoa were sending fleets east, and they would grab the trading rights in every port the crusaders took. In 1099 Venice finally sent a large fleet of its own.

On the way it ran into the Pisan fleet off Rhodes and beat it. The Venetians then stopped at Myra on the coast of Asia Minor, dug up what they said were the bones of St Nicholas, and sent them home to San Nicolò al Lido. In 1100 they helped the crusaders take Haifa before sailing back. Michiel died in 1102.

claims.text: The relics brought to the Lido were the bones of St Nicholas.
claims.note: Sailors from Bari had carried off most of the saint's bones in 1087. The Venetians said they found the rest. Both cities still claim him.

claims.text: The Venetian fleet beat the Pisans off Rhodes in 1099.
claims.note: Described in a Venetian account written soon afterwards. The fight is accepted; the numbers are not.

reigns.hook: Michiel dies. The next doge, Ordelafo Faliero, will build Venice into a sea power, put his face on a golden altarpiece, and die fighting for Zara.

reigns.tagline: The doge on the golden altarpiece, killed at Zara
reigns.previously: Vitale I Michiel dies after sending Venice's first crusade fleet.
paragraphs: Ordelafo Faliero ruled a Venice that was turning itself into a sea power. Tradition says the state shipyard, the Arsenal, was founded in his reign, around 1104. He also had the golden altarpiece of St Mark's, the Pala d'Oro, enlarged with new Byzantine enamels, and a doge's portrait named as his sits on it to this day.

At home, fires swept through the city, and the old island town of Malamocco was swallowed by the sea. In the East a Venetian fleet helped King Baldwin I of Jerusalem take Sidon in 1110, and was paid in trading rights.

Closer to home the kings of Hungary had taken over Croatia and wanted the Dalmatian coast too. In 1117 Faliero led an army to Zara to fight them and was killed in the battle. Venice had lost a doge, and the coast was still in dispute.

claims.text: The Arsenal was founded in 1104.
claims.note: The date is tradition. The shipyard's early history is poorly documented.

claims.text: The doge on the Pala d'Oro really is Ordelafo Faliero.
claims.note: An inscription names him, but some art historians think the figure was reworked in a later restoration, possibly from an emperor's portrait.

reigns.hook: Venice has lost a doge in battle. Domenico Michiel, chosen next, will make peace with Hungary, then sail east with the biggest fleet Venice has ever sent.

reigns.tagline: The terror of the Greeks
reigns.previously: Ordelafo Faliero is killed in battle under the walls of Zara.
paragraphs: Domenico Michiel made a five-year truce with Hungary and turned east. In 1122 he led a great fleet out of the lagoon to help the crusader kingdom of Jerusalem. By the time he got there its king, Baldwin II, was a prisoner of the Turks. Off Jaffa in 1123 the Venetians caught an Egyptian fleet and destroyed it.

For its help Venice was promised a third of the port of Tyre and its own quarter in every town of the kingdom. Tyre fell in 1124 after a long siege. On the way home Michiel settled another score. The emperor John II had refused to renew Venice's golden bull, so the fleet raided Byzantine islands in the Aegean until, in 1126, the emperor gave in.
Michiel stepped down in 1130 and retired to the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore, where he died. His tomb there calls him the terror of the Greeks.

claims.text: His epitaph calls him the terror of the Greeks.
claims.note: The Latin line "Terror Graecorum iacet hic" is on his tomb at San Giorgio Maggiore, though the monument there was remade centuries later.

claims.text: At Tyre he had his ships' rudders taken ashore to prove Venice would not sail away.
claims.note: Told by later Venetian chroniclers. The crusaders' own accounts don't mention it.

claims.text: He paid his men with coins made of leather during the siege.
claims.note: A later Venetian tale, sometimes used to explain the coins on the Michiel family's coat of arms.

reigns.hook: Michiel retires to his monastery. The next doge is his son-in-law, Pietro Polani, who will learn that running Venice through family ties makes enemies fast.

reigns.tagline: The son-in-law who feuded with the Dandolos
reigns.reignEnded: Died after falling ill on campaign
reigns.previously: Domenico Michiel retires to San Giorgio, the terror of the Greeks.
paragraphs: Pietro Polani was married to Domenico Michiel's daughter, and he was generous with jobs for his relatives. That made enemies, above all the Dandolo and Badoer families and their ally the Patriarch of Grado, Enrico Dandolo. The quarrel grew so bitter that Polani drove his Dandolo enemies into exile.

His reign also shows the republic's machinery growing. In 1143 the records first mention a Council of the Wise, a body of leading men who sat beside the doge. It would grow into the Great Council. Venice also fought Padua over the rivers and waterways of the mainland.
In 1147 Roger II of Sicily attacked Byzantium and seized Corfu. Emperor Manuel I called on Venice, and Polani took command of the fleet himself. He fell ill on the way and died in 1148.

claims.text: A Council of the Wise is first recorded beside the doge in 1143.
claims.note: A document of 1143 refers to it. Historians see it as the root of the later Great Council.

claims.text: Polani exiled his Dandolo enemies and had their houses pulled down.
claims.note: Told in the Venetian chronicles. The causes of the feud and how far it went are murky.

reigns.hook: Polani dies before reaching the war. Domenico Morosini takes over and wins it, and the Venetians show the emperor exactly what they think of him.

reigns.tagline: He saved the emperor's island, then mocked the emperor
reigns.previously: Pietro Polani falls ill on campaign against the Normans and dies.
paragraphs: Domenico Morosini took over Polani's war. In 1149 the Venetian fleet helped Manuel I win Corfu back from the Normans. But the allies couldn't stand each other. During the siege Venetian sailors seized the emperor's own ship, dressed an Ethiopian slave in imperial robes and crowned him, to mock Manuel's dark complexion. Manuel never forgot it.

Closer to home, Morosini made Pola and the other towns of Istria swear loyalty to Venice in 1150. He also made peace and a trade deal with William I, the new Norman king of Sicily, which kept the southern seas open to Venetian ships. He died in February 1156.

claims.text: Venetian sailors crowned a slave as a mock emperor to insult Manuel I.
claims.note: Only Niketas Choniates tells the story, writing decades later and no friend of Venice. Most historians accept it.

claims.text: Pola and the Istrian towns swore loyalty to Venice in 1150.
claims.note: The oaths are recorded in Venetian documents of the time.

reigns.hook: Morosini dies with Venetians all over Constantinople, rich, cocky and resented. The new doge, Vitale II Michiel, is about to find out how fast an emperor's favour can turn.

reigns.tagline: He sailed to war and came home to a knife

start.note: elected after the death of his predecessor

reigns.previously: Domenico Morosini dies; Venice is rich and resented in Byzantium.
paragraphs: Vitale II Michiel ran Venice for 15 busy years, backing the Italian cities against the emperor Frederick Barbarossa and keeping the trade flowing. Then, on 12 March 1171, the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos struck. Every Venetian in his empire was arrested on the same day, and their ships, goods and money were seized.

Venice wanted revenge. The doge led a huge fleet east, but instead of fighting he spent the winter negotiating while Manuel's envoys strung him along. Then plague broke out on the crowded ships. In spring 1172 Michiel sailed home with a sick, beaten fleet, and the disease came with him.

The assembly was furious. Michiel left the meeting and headed for the convent of San Zaccaria, but a man caught him in the street nearby and stabbed him to death. It was May 1172. Venice decided that no single man should ever again be able to drag it into such a disaster.

claims.text: Some 10,000 Venetians were arrested in Constantinople alone.
claims.note: The figure comes from Venetian sources keen to stress the outrage. Nobody counted reliably.

claims.text: Plague wrecked the Venetian fleet while the doge negotiated.
claims.note: Both Venetian chronicles and the Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates describe the disease.

claims.text: The assassin's house was pulled down and a ban put on ever rebuilding it in stone.
claims.note: A Venetian tradition attached to a street near San Zaccaria; it isn't recorded at the time.

reigns.hook: Never again will one man lead Venice to ruin. The Venetians rewrite the rules: a small committee will pick the next doge, and it chooses the richest man in the city.

reigns.tagline: The richest man in Venice makes the pope and emperor meet
reigns.previously: Doge Vitale II Michiel is stabbed to death in the street.
paragraphs: After the murder, Venice changed the rules. Instead of the popular assembly acclaiming a doge, a committee of eleven electors chose him, and the people were simply shown the result. Their pick was Sebastiano Ziani, the richest man in Venice. Around this time the Great Council of leading citizens took shape as the real centre of power.

Ziani spent freely. He bought up land and enlarged the Piazza San Marco into something like the square we know. In July 1177 he pulled off a diplomatic triumph. The emperor Frederick Barbarossa, after years of war with the papacy, came to Venice and knelt before Pope Alexander III at the doors of St Mark's. Venice had hosted the peace, and the whole of Europe knew it.

Venetian legend says the grateful pope gave the doge a ring and told him to wed the sea with it every Ascension Day, the start of the Marriage of the Sea. In 1178 the old doge stepped down and retired to a monastery, where he died soon after.

claims.text: Pope Alexander III gave the doge a ring to marry the sea every year.
claims.note: Venetian tradition, celebrated in later paintings in the Doge's Palace. No record from 1177 mentions the gift.

claims.text: Barbarossa knelt and kissed the pope's feet at St Mark's.
claims.note: Archbishop Romuald of Salerno, who was there, describes the scene. The later tale that the pope put his foot on the emperor's neck is legend.

claims.text: Ziani raised the two great columns on the Piazzetta.
claims.note: Tradition puts them in his time; the exact date and who set them up aren't documented.

reigns.hook: Ziani retires to a monastery. The electors turn to Orio Mastropiero, the man who stood aside for him six years ago, and a rebel port on the Dalmatian coast is about to test him.

reigns.tagline: The patient doge who waited six years for the job
reigns.previously: Old Sebastiano Ziani steps down after making Venice the peacemaker.
paragraphs: Orio Mastropiero, whose name is also written Malipiero, had been in line before. In 1172, after Vitale II Michiel's murder, he stood aside for the older and richer Sebastiano Ziani. When Ziani retired in 1178, it was finally his turn.

The big loss of his reign was Zara. Around 1180 the Dalmatian port rebelled again and put itself under the King of Hungary, and Venice couldn't win it back. In Constantinople a mob massacred the city's Latins in 1182. Still, Mastropiero patched up a deal with the new emperor Isaac II in 1187 that restored Venice's trading privileges.

When the Third Crusade set out to win back Jerusalem, Venetian ships joined the siege of Acre. By then the doge was old and tired. In 1192 he gave up the office and retired to the monastery of Santa Croce, where he died on 13 June.

claims.text: Mastropiero stood aside for Sebastiano Ziani in 1172.
claims.note: Venetian chronicles tell it as a model of modesty. The detail rests on their word alone.

claims.text: Zara went over to the King of Hungary around 1180.
claims.note: Hungarian and Venetian sources agree. Venice's failure to retake it set up the Fourth Crusade's attack on Zara in 1202.

reigns.hook: Mastropiero leaves for his monastery. To replace him Venice picks a blind man in his eighties, Enrico Dandolo. He will end up leading a crusade and conquering Constantinople.

reigns.previously: Old Orio Mastropiero retires to a monastery and dies there.
paragraphs: Enrico Dandolo was in his eighties and blind when he was elected in 1192, and still one of the sharpest minds in Venice. In 1201 envoys of the Fourth Crusade asked Venice to build and crew a fleet to carry their army east. The agreed price was 85,000 marks of silver. Venice set aside nearly all its other business to get the ships ready.

Far fewer crusaders turned up than promised, and they couldn't pay. Dandolo offered a deal: help Venice take the rebel city of Zara on the Dalmatian coast, and the debt could wait. Zara fell in 1202. Then a Byzantine prince, Alexios, promised a fortune if they restored his deposed father, Isaac II. The fleet sailed for Constantinople.

In 1203 the old doge stood armed in the prow as his ships ran at the sea walls. When the deal fell apart, the crusaders stormed the city in April 1204, looting it for days and killing many. Venice took a quarter and half a quarter of the empire, plus Crete and the bronze horses now at St Mark's. Dandolo died in Constantinople in 1205 and was buried in Hagia Sophia.

claims.text: The Byzantines blinded Dandolo on an embassy to Constantinople.
claims.note: The story appears in later Venetian chronicles. Villehardouin says he lost his sight from a head wound, and most historians doubt the blinding tale.

claims.text: Dandolo led the assault on the sea walls himself.
claims.note: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, an eyewitness, describes the blind doge in the prow under the banner of St Mark, ordering his men to put him ashore.

claims.text: Dandolo planned all along to steer the crusade to Constantinople.
claims.note: Niketas Choniates blamed Venetian greed and spite. Most modern historians see a chain of debts and accidents instead.

reigns.hook: Dandolo dies in the city he helped conquer. Venice suddenly has an empire of islands and ports to run, and the man who must run it is Pietro Ziani, a doge's son and one of the richest men in Venice.

reigns.tagline: The doge who had to run an empire nobody planned
reigns.previously: Blind old Dandolo dies in Constantinople, buried in Hagia Sophia.
paragraphs: Pietro Ziani was the son of Sebastiano, the richest doge Venice had ever had, and he was very rich himself. He took over in August 1205 with a problem nobody had planned for. Dandolo's crusade had left Venice owning "a quarter and half a quarter" of the Byzantine Empire: harbours, islands and a big slice of Constantinople. The Venetians out there had even picked their own leader, Marino Zeno, who sounded a bit too independent.

Ziani pulled the colonies onto a short lead, with governors sent out from Venice. The big prize was Crete, bought from a crusade leader in 1204 but held by Genoese adventurers, and it took years of fighting to win. From 1211 Venice shipped out colonists, gave them land in return for military service and kept the Greek islanders down by force. Crete stayed Venetian for over 450 years.

Ziani signed trade treaties all round the eastern Mediterranean and kept the galleys busy. In February 1229, old and sick, he stepped down. Choosing the next doge turned into the closest election Venice had yet seen.

claims.text: Ziani proposed moving the capital of the Venetian state to Constantinople, and the idea was defeated by a single vote.
claims.note: Later chronicles tell it and called the result the "vote of Providence". No record of the debate survives from the time.

claims.text: Venice bought its claim to Crete from Boniface of Montferrat in 1204.
claims.note: The agreement survives among Venice's state documents. Actually taking the island meant years of war with the Genoese adventurer Enrico Pescatore.

reigns.hook: The electors split down the middle between Jacopo Tiepolo, the man who first governed Crete, and Marino Dandolo. Venice settles it by drawing lots.

reigns.tagline: Crete's first governor, made doge by the luck of the draw
reigns.cameToPower: Won a tied election by lot
reigns.previously: Old and ill, Pietro Ziani gives up the dogeship in 1229.
paragraphs: Jacopo Tiepolo had done the hard jobs of the new empire. He was the first Venetian duke of Crete, then Venice's chief official in Constantinople. When the electors met in 1229 they split evenly between him and Marino Dandolo. The tie was broken by drawing lots, and Tiepolo won. Venice took the hint and later changed its rules so that a tie could not happen again.

He was a lawmaker's doge. In 1242 he issued a new code of Venetian law, the Statutes, which judges used for centuries. He gave the Dominican friars land for what became the great church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, where he is buried. Crete rebelled again and again, and Venetian fleets kept sailing out to put it down.

Then came the emperor Frederick II, at war with the pope and the Lombard cities. Venice backed the cities. Tiepolo's son Pietro, governor of Milan, was captured at Cortenuova in 1237, paraded in triumph and later put to death. Worn out, the doge abdicated in May 1249 and died that July.

claims.text: The 1229 election ended in a dead tie, broken by drawing lots.
claims.note: The tie is told in the Venetian chronicles, including Andrea Dandolo's. The exact vote count rests on those later accounts.

claims.text: Frederick II paraded the captured Pietro Tiepolo into Cremona on Milan's war cart, and later had him executed.
claims.note: Frederick boasted of the Cremona triumph in his letters, and chroniclers record Pietro's execution at Trani in 1240.

reigns.hook: Venice tinkers with its election rules so there are no more ties. The next pick is a safe pair of hands in his late sixties: Marino Morosini.

reigns.tagline: A calm old man after two stormy reigns
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by a college of electors
reigns.previously: Jacopo Tiepolo abdicates in May 1249 and dies that July.
paragraphs: After two long and eventful reigns, Venice wanted calm. Marino Morosini, from one of the city's oldest families, was elected in June 1249 in his late sixties. The choice went through a college of electors set up so it could never split evenly again. Each new doge also swore a longer oath of office, the promissione, spelling out what he could not do. Doges were becoming chairmen rather than princes.

Morosini got his calm. The emperor Frederick II, the great enemy of the last reign, died in December 1250, and the wars in Lombardy wound down. Venetian galleys kept trading east from the ports Dandolo had won. Morosini died on 1 January 1253 after three and a half years, a doge remembered mainly for keeping things quiet.

claims.text: Morosini was one of the first doges chosen by a college of 41 electors, an odd number to stop ties.
claims.note: Some lists date the college of 41 to his election in 1249, others to the reform of 1268. The exact year is uncertain.

reigns.hook: Morosini dies on New Year's Day 1253. His successor, Reniero Zeno, is about to spend fifteen years fighting Genoa.

reigns.tagline: War with Genoa, and Constantinople lost
reigns.previously: Old Marino Morosini dies on New Year's Day 1253.
paragraphs: Reniero Zeno was a seasoned soldier and envoy, and he needed to be. In 1256 Venetians and Genoese in Acre, the crusader port in the Holy Land, came to blows over a property of the monastery of St Sabas. It turned into a full war. A Venetian fleet under Lorenzo Tiepolo forced its way into Acre harbour and burned Genoese ships, and in 1258 Venice beat Genoa in a sea battle off the port.

Genoa found a cleverer weapon. In 1261 it allied with the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII, and that July his troops slipped into Constantinople and took it back from the Latins. The Latin emperor fled on a Venetian ship. Venice lost its favoured place in the city its crusaders had stormed in 1204, and the Genoese moved in.
Venice fought back at sea and won again in 1263 and 1266, but it could not undo the loss. Zeno died on 7 July 1268. His death set off a rethink of how the next doge should be chosen.

claims.text: Two carved pillars beside St Mark's were loot from Genoa's quarter in Acre, taken after the victory of 1258.
claims.note: Venetians long called them the Pillars of Acre. Excavations in Istanbul in the 1960s showed they came from the church of St Polyeuktos in Constantinople, probably taken in 1204.

claims.text: The war began over a property belonging to the monastery of St Sabas in Acre.
claims.note: Venetian and Genoese chroniclers both trace the fighting to the dispute, and the war is named after it.

reigns.hook: Venice now builds an election machine of lotteries and votes so tangled that nobody can rig it. The first doge it produces is the hero of Acre, Lorenzo Tiepolo.

reigns.tagline: The first doge out of the lottery machine
reigns.previously: Reniero Zeno dies after fifteen years of war with Genoa.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Tiepolo was a war hero and a doge's son. He had led the fleet that broke into Acre harbour in the war with Genoa. In July 1268 he became the first doge picked by Venice's new election system, a long chain of lotteries and votes inside the Great Council that ended with 41 electors. It was built so that no family could fix the result, and it lasted until 1797.

His election party was remembered for years. The chronicler Martin da Canal described the guilds of Venice parading before the new doge one after another, each in its finery, with banners and trumpets, to greet him at the palace.

There was trouble too: a quarrel with Bologna over trade on the rivers, and Genoa still prowling. In 1271 the merchants Niccolò and Maffeo Polo set out east again, taking Niccolò's teenage son Marco. Tiepolo died on 15 August 1275.

claims.text: The guilds of Venice paraded before Lorenzo Tiepolo after his election.
claims.note: Described in detail by Martin da Canal in Les Estoires de Venise, written in French at the time.

claims.text: Tiepolo was the first doge chosen by the election procedure of 1268.
claims.note: The procedure is set out in the Great Council's decrees of 1268 and was used, with small changes, until 1797.

reigns.hook: Tiepolo dies in August 1275. The machine grinds into action again and produces a doge of about 80, Jacopo Contarini.

reigns.tagline: Elected at about 80, worn out by a war at sea
reigns.previously: Lorenzo Tiepolo, first doge of the 1268 ballot, dies.
paragraphs: Jacopo Contarini was about 81 when he was elected in September 1275, from a family that gave Venice eight doges in all. Venice now claimed to police the whole Adriatic, which it called its Gulf, and made ships trading there pay tolls and call at Venice. Other ports hated it.

Ancona, the busiest port on the Italian side, pushed back hardest, and the quarrel turned into a long and costly war at sea. By March 1280 the old doge had had enough. He asked to step down, and on 6 March the councils let him go. He died later that year.

claims.text: Contarini resigned simply because he was too old.
claims.note: The chronicles give his age as the reason. Some historians think the unpopular Ancona war helped push him out.

claims.text: Venice claimed the right to control shipping across the whole Adriatic.
claims.note: Venetian treaties and toll rules of the 13th century show it, and Venice kept pressing the claim for centuries.

reigns.hook: Contarini retires. The electors pick Giovanni Dandolo, who is away from the city on state business. Under him, Venice will strike its first gold coin.

reigns.tagline: The doge of the very first gold ducat
reigns.previously: Old Jacopo Contarini retires in March 1280, worn out.
paragraphs: Giovanni Dandolo was away serving the Republic when the electors chose him in March 1280, and he came home to a job full of trouble. The towns of Istria were restless, and the Patriarch of Aquileia, a churchman who ruled the lands next door, backed them. Venice spent years fighting along the Istrian coast.

His lasting mark was in people's purses. In 1284 the Great Council ordered a gold coin to rival Florence's florin: the ducat, about 3.5 grams of almost pure gold, showing the doge kneeling before St Mark. Venice kept it at the same weight and purity for five centuries, and traders all over the Mediterranean trusted it.
Dandolo died in office on 2 November 1289. The crowd in the piazza already knew who it wanted next. The electors had other ideas.

claims.text: The first gold ducats were struck in 1284, under Giovanni Dandolo.
claims.note: A Great Council decree of 1284 ordered the coin, and ducats bearing Dandolo's name survive in museums.

claims.text: The ducat kept the same weight and gold content until the Republic fell.
claims.note: Coin studies show about 3.5 grams of nearly pure gold from 1284 to 1797.

reigns.hook: Dandolo dies in office. The people cheer for Giacomo Tiepolo, son and grandson of doges, but the electors want someone else: Pietro Gradenigo, not yet 40.

reigns.tagline: The doge who locked the doors of the Great Council
reigns.cameToPower: Elected, though the crowd wanted another
reigns.previously: Giovanni Dandolo, doge of the first gold ducat, dies in office.
paragraphs: The crowd in the piazza wanted Giacomo Tiepolo, son and grandson of doges. The electors chose Pietro Gradenigo, about 38, from an old family, and the people never warmed to him. In 1291 Acre fell to the Mamluks, the last crusader port in the Holy Land. In 1298 Genoa smashed a Venetian fleet at Curzola, off the Dalmatian coast. Marco Polo ended up in a Genoese jail around then, and dictated his travels to a cellmate.

In February 1297 (still 1296 in Venice, whose year began on 1 March) came the Serrata, the "closing". Seats on the Great Council went to men whose families had sat there lately, and over the next years it hardened into a rule: if your father was in, you were in. If not, you were out for good. This was the birth of the Venetian nobility, and it lasted until 1797.

Shut-out families and old rivals seethed. A war over Ferrara got Venice hit with a papal interdict in 1309. On 15 June 1310 Bajamonte Tiepolo and the Querini family marched on the piazza to topple the doge. A storm, bad timing and loyal militia broke the revolt. To hunt down the plotters, the government set up a special court of ten men. It was meant to last a few months.

claims.text: An old woman dropped a stone mortar from her window, killing the rebels' standard-bearer and starting the rout.
claims.note: A carved relief near the Merceria still marks the spot, but the details, including her name, come from later chronicles.

claims.text: Marco Polo was captured at the battle of Curzola.
claims.note: Giovanni Battista Ramusio said so in the 16th century. Some historians place his capture in a smaller clash a couple of years earlier.

claims.text: The Serrata was passed in February 1297.
claims.note: The law survives in the Great Council's records, dated 1296 by the Venetian calendar.

reigns.hook: Gradenigo dies in 1311 with Venice under a papal interdict. The Council of Ten was meant as a stopgap, but it stays. To calm things, the electors pick a gentle old man: Marino Zorzi.

reigns.tagline: A kindly old man, doge for less than a year
reigns.previously: Gradenigo dies in 1311; his emergency Council of Ten lives on.
paragraphs: Venice in 1311 was in a bad way. The war over Ferrara had been lost, the pope's interdict still hung over the city and its trade, and the Tiepolo plotters had only just been scattered. The electors went for comfort: Marino Zorzi, about 80, known for his charity rather than his politics.

There was no calm to be had. The Dalmatian city of Zara threw off Venetian rule and turned to the king of Hungary. Zorzi had no time to deal with it, or with anything else. He died on 3 July 1312, less than eleven months after his election, and the Council of Ten kept sitting.

claims.text: Zorzi was famous for his charity, especially to prisoners and the poor.
claims.note: This is the reputation the chronicles give him. Little else is recorded of him, and it may be partly pious decoration.

claims.text: Zara rebelled against Venice in 1311 and went over to Hungary.
claims.note: Venetian and Dalmatian records agree; Venice won the city back in 1313.

reigns.hook: Zorzi's reign is over almost before it starts. Next comes a hard old sailor, Giovanni Soranzo, who once took a fleet into the Black Sea and seized Genoa's colony at Caffa.

reigns.tagline: The admiral who raided the Black Sea, then made peace
reigns.previously: Kindly old Marino Zorzi dies after less than a year.
paragraphs: Giovanni Soranzo had made his name at sea. In 1296, during a war with Genoa, he led a Venetian fleet into the Black Sea and took the Genoese colony of Caffa in Crimea. Elected in July 1312, he set about repairing the damage of the last few years. In 1313 the pope lifted the interdict, once Venice had made peace over Ferrara and paid up, and Zara was brought back under Venetian rule.
His sixteen years were mostly peaceful and good for business. State-owned galleys sailed in convoys east to the Levant and, before long, west to Flanders and England too. Venice got richer.

There was a private cost. His own son-in-law was among the exiled plotters of 1310, and the doge could do nothing for him. With the Council of Ten watching, family ties counted for little. Soranzo died on the last day of 1328.

claims.text: Soranzo captured the Genoese colony of Caffa in 1296.
claims.note: Venetian and Genoese chroniclers both record the raid; Venice did not hold the town for long.

claims.text: Venice's state galley convoys to Flanders began during his reign.
claims.note: Frederic Lane dates the first regular Flanders voyages to the 1310s; the exact first year is debated.

reigns.hook: Soranzo dies on New Year's Eve 1328. The electors turn to the diplomat who got the interdict lifted, a man with an odd nickname: Francesco Dandolo, "the Dog".

reigns.tagline: The ambassador they called the Dog
reigns.previously: Giovanni Soranzo, the old admiral, dies on New Year's Eve 1328.
paragraphs: Francesco Dandolo was the man who had talked the pope round. Around 1310 Venice sent him to Clement V at Avignon to plead for an end to the interdict that was strangling Venetian trade. It took years of begging, but it worked, and Venice never forgot. In January 1329 it made him doge.

In 1335 the Council of Ten, set up in 1310 for one emergency, was made permanent. Plots, spies and the safety of the state belonged to the Ten from now on. Dandolo's big venture was on the mainland. Venice and Florence went to war with Mastino della Scala, lord of Verona, who was choking Venetian trade on the rivers. The peace of 1339 gave Venice Treviso, its first lasting city on the mainland.
Dandolo died on 31 October 1339 and was buried in the Frari church. A painted lunette by Paolo Veneziano from his tomb shows him and his wife kneeling before the Virgin.

claims.text: Dandolo crawled under the pope's table in a dog's collar to win pardon for Venice, and was nicknamed "the Dog".
claims.note: The scene appears in later Venetian chronicles. The nickname Cane may have been a family name, with the story invented to explain it.

claims.text: The Council of Ten was made permanent in 1335.
claims.note: The decision is in the council records in the Venetian State Archives.

reigns.hook: Dandolo dies with Treviso won. His successor, Bartolomeo Gradenigo, is already 76, and his short reign will be remembered for one terrible night of storm.
