reigns.tagline: A storm, a fisherman and St Mark's ring
reigns.previously: Francesco Dandolo dies, with Treviso now Venetian.
paragraphs: Bartolomeo Gradenigo was 76 when he was elected in November 1339, from the same old family as Pietro Gradenigo, the doge of the Serrata. Nobody expected a long reign, and he didn't have one. Venice was rich, confident and busy settling into its new mainland city of Treviso.

His reign is remembered for a storm. In February 1340 a huge gale and tide battered the lagoon. Venetians told how, that night, three strangers made a fisherman row them out into the storm, where they sank a ship full of demons bearing down on the city. They were Saints Mark, George and Nicholas, and St Mark gave the fisherman his ring to show the doge.
Two centuries later Paris Bordone painted the fisherman handing over the ring, a picture now in the Accademia in Venice. Gradenigo died on 28 December 1342, after just over three years.

claims.text: St Mark, St George and St Nicholas saved Venice from a storm of demons and left the doge St Mark's ring.
claims.note: A pious story from the Venetian chronicles. Paris Bordone's painting of about 1534 in the Accademia shows the fisherman presenting the ring.

claims.text: A great storm and flood struck Venice in February 1340.
claims.note: Venetian chronicles record the storm, which is why the legend was attached to it.

reigns.hook: With Gradenigo gone, the electors reach for a man half his age: Andrea Dandolo, a bookish young scholar who will write Venice's history as well as run it.

reigns.tagline: The scholar doge who wrote Venice's history
reigns.previously: Old Bartolomeo Gradenigo dies after three years as doge.
paragraphs: Andrea Dandolo came from the blind crusader doge's family. At about 36 he was a baby by Venetian standards, and a real intellectual. He collected the city's laws into a new book of statutes and wrote chronicles of Venice from its first doges to his own day. He had the golden altarpiece of St Mark's, the Pala d'Oro, reset in a grand new frame. The poet Petrarch was a friend and wrote him letters.

Then came 1348. The Black Death arrived on merchant ships and tore through the crowded city. Boats carried the dead out to burial pits on lagoon islands. Venice appointed health officials to fight it, the start of public health rules the world would later copy. Barely recovered, Venice went to war with Genoa again in 1350. Petrarch wrote to Dandolo begging for peace. Nobody listened.

Dandolo died in September 1354, not yet 50, with the war going badly. He was buried in the baptistery of St Mark's, which he had covered in mosaics. This time the electors wanted an old, steady hand. They picked a man of about 70 who wasn't even in Venice.

claims.text: The Black Death killed up to three-fifths of Venice's people.
claims.note: That figure comes from chroniclers. Modern estimates vary widely, though everyone agrees the city lost a huge share of its population.

claims.text: Petrarch wrote to Dandolo pleading for peace with Genoa.
claims.note: The letters survive in Petrarch's collected correspondence.

reigns.hook: The new doge is Marino Faliero, a war hero and diplomat of about 70. He sails home to take up the job. Within months he'll try to make himself master of Venice.

reigns.tagline: The doge they beheaded and painted out of history
reigns.cameToPower: Elected while away as an envoy
reigns.previously: Andrea Dandolo dies with the war against Genoa going badly.
paragraphs: Marino Faliero had done it all: commander, governor, ambassador. He was away on a mission to the papal court when he heard he'd been elected. He reached Venice in October 1354, and within weeks the Genoese wiped out a Venetian fleet at Porto Longo in Greece. Then a young noble, Michele Steno, scribbled an insult about the doge and his wife, and the judges let him off lightly. The old man was furious.

In April 1355 he plotted with commoners, seamen and shipyard men who had their own grudges against the nobles. The plan was to stir up panic, kill the leading nobles in the piazza and make Faliero lord of Venice. Someone talked. The Council of Ten rounded up the plotters, hanged several from the palace windows, and then put the doge himself on trial.

On 17 April 1355 Faliero was beheaded at the top of the palace stairs where he had sworn his oath. His memory was wiped. In the Great Council hall, where every doge has a portrait, his place shows a painted black cloth and Latin words: this is the place of Marino Faliero, beheaded for his crimes. Byron wrote a play about him in 1821, and Donizetti an opera.

claims.text: The plot began with Steno's insult and the doge's rage at his light sentence.
claims.note: The story comes from later chronicles. The trial records give no clear motive, and the wording of the insult changes with every telling.

claims.text: Faliero was beheaded on the Giants' Staircase.
claims.note: A popular telling, but that staircase was built in the late 15th century, over a hundred years later.

claims.text: His place in the frieze of doges is a painted black cloth.
claims.note: It is still there. The present frieze was painted after the fire of 1577, but it repeats the old blank.

reigns.hook: Faliero's head rolls on the palace stairs. The shaken electors want someone safe, and they turn to old Giovanni Gradenigo, from a family that has run Venice before.

reigns.tagline: The old man who took the chair Faliero lost
reigns.previously: Doge Marino Faliero is beheaded for plotting to make himself lord.
paragraphs: Four days after Faliero's head rolled, the electors wanted a safe pair of hands. They found one in Giovanni Gradenigo, a man in his seventies from one of the oldest noble clans in the city. His family had already given Venice two doges, including Pietro Gradenigo, who had locked the Great Council to newcomers. Nobody expected this one to plot anything.

The Council of Ten, which had crushed Faliero's plot, now sat at the centre of power, and the new doge let it. His big job was ending the war with Genoa, and peace was signed in June 1355. Calm did not last. King Louis I of Hungary wanted the Dalmatian coast back, and in 1356 his armies marched into Venetian lands around Treviso. Gradenigo died that August with the war barely begun.

claims.text: Gradenigo was nicknamed Nasone, "Big Nose".
claims.note: The nickname appears in later lists of the doges. Nothing from his own time explains it.

claims.text: Peace with Genoa was signed in June 1355, weeks into his reign.
claims.note: The treaty, made with Milan's ruling Visconti as go-between, is well documented in Venetian records.

reigns.hook: The Hungarians are camped round Treviso. Inside the town is the Venetian commander, Giovanni Dolfin, and the electors are about to give him the strangest promotion in the republic's history.

reigns.tagline: Elected under siege, he had to fight his way home
reigns.previously: Giovanni Gradenigo dies just as Hungary invades Venice's mainland.
paragraphs: When the news came that he was doge, Giovanni Dolfin was stuck inside Treviso with a Hungarian army all round it. The king of Hungary would not let him pass. So Dolfin rode out with a small band of horsemen, broke through the lines and reached the lagoon to take his oath. It was a dashing start to a gloomy reign.

The war went badly. Hungary held the Dalmatian ports and squeezed Venice's mainland. In February 1358 the Treaty of Zara gave the whole coast from the Gulf of Quarnero to Durazzo to King Louis I. The doge even had to drop "Duke of Dalmatia" from his title, a name his predecessors had worn for over 350 years. Dolfin lived on for three quieter years and died in July 1361.

claims.text: Dolfin had lost an eye in battle before he became doge.
claims.note: Later chroniclers say so, and some portraits hint at it, but no record from his own time confirms it.

claims.text: Dolfin cut his way out of besieged Treviso to take office.
claims.note: Venetian chronicles agree he left the town by force, though they differ on how many men rode with him.

claims.text: The Treaty of Zara made Venice give up Dalmatia and the doge's Dalmatian title.
claims.note: The treaty text survives. Venice won the coast back by purchase in 1409.

reigns.hook: Dolfin is dead. The man chosen next is out at sea with the fleet, and his own father is said to be so jealous of the honour that he won't take off his cap to him.

reigns.tagline: The young doge who threw a party Petrarch watched
reigns.previously: Giovanni Dolfin dies, three years after losing Dalmatia to Hungary.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Celsi was about 50, young for a doge, and he was away commanding galleys when the electors picked him. He liked pomp and a showy court, and some nobles muttered that he behaved more like a prince than an elected official. In 1363 the Venetian settlers of Crete, angry at taxes, rose with the Greeks in the Revolt of St Titus and declared their own republic.

Venice hired a Lombard captain, Luchino dal Verme, and crushed the rising in the spring of 1364. Celsi threw a huge victory party with jousts in the Piazza San Marco. The poet Petrarch, then living in Venice, sat beside the doge on the basilica's loggia and wrote a letter describing it all. When Celsi died in July 1365, the Ten looked into rumours that he had dreamed of making himself lord.

claims.text: Celsi's father refused to bow to his son, so the doge put a cross on his cap to make him bow to that.
claims.note: A favourite story of later chroniclers, with no support in records of the time.

claims.text: Petrarch watched the 1364 victory celebrations from beside the doge.
claims.note: Petrarch describes the tournament himself in a letter in his Seniles.

claims.text: Celsi was secretly plotting to seize power when he died.
claims.note: An inquiry after his death is mentioned in some sources, but its findings are unclear and he was never condemned.

reigns.hook: After the showman, the electors want someone humble. They pick a man nearly 80, from the poorer branch of a great family.

reigns.tagline: An old ambassador gets the top job at nearly 80
reigns.previously: Lorenzo Celsi dies, dogged by rumours that he wanted to be a prince.
paragraphs: Marco Corner had spent his life on missions for the republic, to popes, emperors and kings. He came from a less well-off branch of the rich Corner clan, and at the election his rivals sneered at how little money he had. It made no difference. After the high living of Celsi, a modest old servant of the state looked just right.

The last rebels on Crete were hunted down in his time. At home the Great Council hall got a vast new fresco of Paradise by Guariento of Padua across its end wall. It was later covered by Tintoretto's own Paradise, but scraps of it survive. Corner died in January 1368 after two and a half years. His tomb, with statues by Nino Pisano, is in the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo.

claims.text: Corner's poverty was raised against him at his election.
claims.note: Told by Venetian chroniclers, who give him a proud reply. The exact words vary and may be invented.

claims.text: Guariento's Paradise was painted during Corner's reign.
claims.note: It is usually dated 1365 to 1368, but the start may come earlier under Celsi.

reigns.hook: The electors turn next to Andrea Contarini, who doesn't want the job at all. They'll have to threaten him to make him take it.

reigns.tagline: The reluctant doge who saved Venice at Chioggia
reigns.previously: Marco Corner dies in his eighties after under three years.
paragraphs: Andrea Contarini was elderly and wanted nothing to do with the job. He said no, and was told to accept or face exile and lose his property. He took it. Ten years later Venice and Genoa went to war again over Tenedos, an island at the mouth of the Dardanelles. It became the War of Chioggia, the nearest Venice came to being conquered before Napoleon.

In 1379 the Genoese, with the lord of Padua and the king of Hungary on their side, smashed a Venetian fleet at Pola. In August they seized Chioggia at the lagoon's southern tip. Venice was blockaded and hungry. The people demanded Vettor Pisani, the admiral jailed for losing at Pola. He was let out and put in charge, and the old doge went aboard the fleet himself.

Venice sank blockships in the channels and trapped the Genoese inside Chioggia. On 1 January 1380 Carlo Zeno sailed in from the east with a fresh fleet, and in June the starving Genoese surrendered. The Peace of Turin in 1381 ended the war. Thirty families who had helped pay for it were rewarded with seats on the Great Council. Contarini died in June 1382.

claims.text: Contarini was threatened with exile and confiscation to make him take the job.
claims.note: Told by Venetian chroniclers. Refusing office was punishable under Venetian law, but the details of his case are thin.

claims.text: Crowds forced the release of Vettor Pisani.
claims.note: Chronicles of the war describe the people refusing to row without him.

claims.text: Thirty new families joined the Great Council in 1381.
claims.note: Recorded in the council's own acts. It was the last big intake until places were sold in the 17th century.

reigns.hook: Genoa never really recovers. Venice picks one of its richest men, Michele Morosini, to rebuild, but plague is already in the city.

reigns.tagline: Four months as doge, then the plague came
reigns.previously: Chioggia is saved, Genoa is beaten, and old Contarini dies.
paragraphs: Michele Morosini was one of the richest men in Venice and from one of its grandest families. After the War of Chioggia the electors wanted a man of means to rebuild. Venice was broke, its trade battered and its island of Tenedos handed over to neutral keeping by the peace treaty.

He never got the chance. Plague broke out in the city that summer, and on 16 October 1382, four months after his election, the doge died of it. He was buried in Santi Giovanni e Paolo, where his tomb still stands. His reign is one of the shortest in the list.

claims.text: During the war Morosini bought houses cheap while others panicked, and boasted that if Venice fell he would not care.
claims.note: The story comes from later writers. Some tell it to show his greed, others say he bought to show faith in the city.

claims.text: Morosini died of plague.
claims.note: Chronicles give plague as the cause, and there was an outbreak in Venice that year.

reigns.hook: Morosini's death leaves the cap empty again. This time the electors pick a man who is far away, governing Crete, and who will rule with an iron sense of justice.

reigns.tagline: The doge who let his own son die in prison
reigns.previously: Michele Morosini dies of plague after just four months.
paragraphs: Antonio Venier was running Crete as its duke when he was elected, and it took weeks for him to sail home. He then ruled for 18 years, and Venice spent them picking up ports. In 1386 Corfu put itself under Venetian rule, guarding the mouth of the Adriatic. Argos and Nauplia in Greece followed, bought or handed over as their lords ran out of options.

He is best remembered for a grim story. His son Alvise was jailed for insulting a noble family, and when the young man fell ill in prison, the doge refused to have him released. Alvise died in his cell. Venetians held Venier up as the model of a ruler who put the law above his family. He died in November 1400.

claims.text: Venier refused to free his dying son from prison.
claims.note: Told by chroniclers as a lesson in justice. The offence and the details of the death vary between versions.

claims.text: Corfu came under Venetian rule in 1386.
claims.note: The island's leaders accepted Venetian rule that year, and Venice held it until 1797.

reigns.hook: Next comes Michele Steno, the man chroniclers say once scrawled the insult that drove Faliero to treason. As an old doge, he'll make Venice a land power.

reigns.tagline: The insulter of Faliero, now the doge who took Padua
reigns.previously: Antonio Venier dies after 18 years of hard justice.
paragraphs: Half a century earlier, so the story goes, a cocky young Michele Steno had scribbled a filthy joke about Doge Faliero and his wife. Now he was doge himself, a wealthy old noble who loved fine things. He chose his moment well. In 1402 Gian Galeazzo Visconti, the duke of Milan, died, and his empire in northern Italy fell apart.

Venice moved in. Vicenza handed itself over in 1404. Verona and Padua were taken in 1405 after a hard war with the Carrara lords of Padua, old enemies from Chioggia. In January 1406 Francesco Novello da Carrara and two of his sons were strangled in their Venetian prison. In 1409 Venice bought the rights to Dalmatia for 100,000 ducats. Steno died in December 1413, master of a mainland state.

claims.text: Doge Steno was the young man who insulted Faliero.
claims.note: Chroniclers made the link, but the insult story is shaky, so the identification is too.

claims.text: The Council of Ten had the Carrara lords killed in prison.
claims.note: Well documented in Venetian records, though the official line at the time was that they died naturally.

claims.text: Venice bought Dalmatia for 100,000 ducats in 1409.
claims.note: The deal with Ladislaus of Naples, who claimed the Hungarian throne, is well recorded.

reigns.hook: Steno's successor is a merchant who thinks war is bad for business. He will spend his last breath warning Venice about the man who wants his job.

reigns.tagline: The merchant doge who warned Venice from his deathbed
reigns.previously: Michele Steno dies with Padua and Verona under the lion.
paragraphs: Tommaso Mocenigo was about 70, a veteran sea commander and diplomat. He believed in trade, peace and balanced books. Still, his reign added land. In 1420 Venice took Friuli from the patriarch of Aquileia, and the towns of the Dalmatian coast came under the lion too. Venetian galleys ran regular convoys to Flanders, Egypt and the Black Sea, and money poured in.

As he lay dying in April 1423, Mocenigo is said to have called in the leading nobles for a last speech. He reeled off figures: ships, sailors, ducats, rents. Peace, he told them, had made Venice rich. Then he named the man they must not elect, Francesco Foscari, an ambitious procurator who loved war and spent freely. Days after the funeral, they elected Foscari.

claims.text: Mocenigo gave a deathbed speech warning against Foscari, packed with figures on Venice's trade.
claims.note: The text survives in Marino Sanudo's lives of the doges and other copies. Some historians think it was polished or written up later by Foscari's enemies.

reigns.hook: Venice ignores the dying doge. Francesco Foscari takes the ducal cap and keeps it for 34 years, the longest reign of any doge, with the cruellest ending.

reigns.tagline: The longest-reigning doge, forced out at the end
reigns.previously: Mocenigo dies warning Venice never to elect Francesco Foscari.
paragraphs: Foscari did just what Mocenigo feared. For thirty years Venice fought the Visconti dukes of Milan, and the border crept west to Brescia and Bergamo. The fighting was done by hired generals, the condottieri. One of them, Carmagnola, was suspected of double-dealing. In 1432 the Ten lured him to Venice, tried him in secret and beheaded him between the columns of the Piazzetta.

In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, where Venetians had traded for centuries. The Peace of Lodi in 1454 brought a rough balance to Italy. But Foscari's family was falling apart. His son Jacopo was accused of taking bribes, then of murder, then of treason. The Council of Ten had him tortured and exiled three times. He died on Crete in 1457.

The doge, past 80 and crushed by grief, stopped turning up to councils. In October 1457 the Ten told him to step down. He refused, then gave in, and on 23 October left the palace for his family home on the Grand Canal. He died on 1 November. Byron turned the story into a play, The Two Foscari, and Verdi into an opera.

claims.text: Foscari died after hearing the bells ring for his successor.
claims.note: Pasquale Malipiero was elected days before Foscari died, so the timing roughly fits, but the scene comes from later retellings.

claims.text: Carmagnola really was betraying Venice.
claims.note: The Ten convicted him in secret. Historians still argue whether he was a traitor or just a cautious general.

claims.text: Jacopo Foscari was tortured and exiled three times on the Ten's orders.
claims.note: The trials are in the Ten's records and well covered by historians, including Dennis Romano.

reigns.hook: Foscari is gone. The electors pick mild Pasquale Malipiero, while the old doge is still alive in his house on the Grand Canal.

reigns.tagline: The calm doge chosen while Foscari still lived
reigns.cameToPower: Elected after Foscari was forced out
reigns.previously: Foscari, forced out after 34 years, is made to leave the palace.
paragraphs: Pasquale Malipiero was elected a week after the Ten pushed Francesco Foscari out of office. Two days later the old doge died, and Venice gave him a full doge's funeral anyway. Malipiero was a mild man, and after 34 years of Foscari's wars, that was the point. The city wanted a breather.

It got one. Italy was mostly at peace under the Peace of Lodi, and Venice kept out of trouble. In 1459 Pope Pius II called the Christian powers to Mantua to plan a crusade against the Ottomans. Venice sent polite words and very little else, since war would wreck its trade with the sultan. Malipiero died in May 1462. His tomb in Santi Giovanni e Paolo was carved by the Lombardo workshop.

claims.text: Malipiero's wife, Giovanna Dandolo, encouraged lace-making and printing in Venice.
claims.note: Later Venetian writers praised her as a patron of both, but evidence from her own time is thin.

claims.text: Foscari died two days after Malipiero's election.
claims.note: Malipiero was chosen on 30 October 1457; Foscari died on 1 November.

reigns.hook: Malipiero leaves a quiet republic behind. His successor, Cristoforo Moro, will not be so lucky: the pope wants him on a crusade, in person.

reigns.tagline: The reluctant crusader who sailed to meet a dying pope
reigns.previously: Pasquale Malipiero dies after five years of rare peace.
paragraphs: Cristoforo Moro was pious and cautious, and he did not want a war. He got one. The Ottomans kept nibbling at Venetian outposts in Greece, and in 1463 Venice declared war on Sultan Mehmed II. It would last sixteen years. Pope Pius II, still keen on his crusade, now had an ally, and he wanted the doge himself to sail with the fleet.

Moro said he was too old, but the Senate told him to go. In August 1464 the Venetian galleys reached Ancona, where the sick pope was waiting to lead the crusade. Pius died there days later, and the whole plan fell apart. The war went on without him. In 1470 Mehmed took Negroponte, Venice's great base in the Aegean. Moro died in November 1471 and was buried in San Giobbe, a church he paid to rebuild.

claims.text: Moro was ordered by the Senate to join the crusade in person.
claims.note: Venetian chroniclers record a councillor telling him he would be made to go if he would not go willingly.

claims.text: Pius II died just as the Venetian galleys came into Ancona.
claims.note: He died on 14 August 1464. Chroniclers say he saw the fleet arrive from his window, which may be a touch of drama.

reigns.hook: The next doge made his fortune trading in Rhodes. He'll put his own face on Venice's new silver coin, and the republic won't like it.

reigns.tagline: The doge whose face was too big for the coins
reigns.previously: Cristoforo Moro dies with Negroponte lost and the Turkish war raging.
paragraphs: Nicolò Tron had grown very rich as a merchant on Rhodes, and he came home to a city at war with the sultan. In 1472 Venice brought out a big new silver coin worth one lira, and it carried a true-to-life portrait of the doge. Venetians soon called it the lira tron. Nobody had put a doge's real face on a coin before, and some nobles thought it looked far too much like a king.

Meanwhile Venice played a long game in Cyprus. Its king, James II, had married a Venetian noblewoman, Caterina Cornaro, and the republic declared her its daughter. When James died in 1473, Venice's fleet was close at hand to protect the young widow and her claim. Tron died in July 1473. His grand tomb by Antonio Rizzo fills a wall of the Frari church.

claims.text: The lira tron was the first Venetian coin with a realistic portrait of the doge.
claims.note: Coin collections hold many examples. Later doges went back to the stiff kneeling figure.

claims.text: Portraits of doges on coins were stopped because they looked too princely.
claims.note: That is the usual explanation, but no law spelling it out is clearly recorded.

reigns.hook: Tron is dead and the Turks are on the move in Albania. The next doge, Nicolò Marcello, will have just 16 months.

reigns.tagline: Sixteen months, a siege survived and a coin
reigns.previously: Nicolò Tron dies as Cyprus slips into Venice's hands.
paragraphs: Nicolò Marcello was in his seventies and had spent his life in the republic's offices. He took office with the Ottoman war in its tenth year. In 1474 a big Ottoman army besieged Scutari, a Venetian town in Albania. Its commander, Antonio Loredan, held out through the summer heat as food and water ran short. The Ottomans gave up and marched away.

In Cyprus the baby king James III, son of Caterina Cornaro, died in 1474, and Venetian officers now ran the island in his mother's name. At home a new half-lira silver coin was named the marcello after the doge. Marcello died on 1 December 1474. His tomb by Pietro Lombardo now stands in Santi Giovanni e Paolo.

claims.text: Loredan told his starving men they could eat his own flesh before they surrendered.
claims.note: A famous heroic story of the siege, told by later writers. No eyewitness record confirms it.

claims.text: The marcello coin was named after the doge.
claims.note: The coin, worth half a lira, was first struck in his reign and kept his name for decades.

reigns.hook: Marcello is dead. His successor, Pietro Mocenigo, is the admiral who has been burning Ottoman ports and keeping Cyprus safe for Caterina Cornaro.

reigns.tagline: The admiral who came home to wear the cap
reigns.previously: Nicolò Marcello dies after sixteen months, with Scutari saved.
paragraphs: Pietro Mocenigo was a fighting man. After Negroponte fell in 1470, Venice made him captain general of the sea, and he took the war to the sultan. With papal and Neapolitan galleys alongside, he raided the Ottoman coasts of Asia Minor and burned the port of Smyrna in 1472.

Then came a gift of an island. King James II of Cyprus died in 1473, leaving a Venetian widow, Caterina Cornaro, who was expecting his child. Nobles hostile to Venice tried to seize power. Mocenigo sailed in, put the plot down and made sure Caterina stayed queen, with Venice right behind her throne.

Elected doge in December 1474, he got only fourteen months in the job. He died on 23 February 1476. His family gave him one of the great tombs of Venice, by Pietro Lombardo in Santi Giovanni e Paolo. It shows him standing in armour, more general than doge.

claims.text: His tomb says it was paid for from the spoils of his enemies.
claims.note: The Latin inscription on the monument reads EX HOSTIUM MANUBIIS, 'from the spoils of the enemy'.

claims.text: Mocenigo's fleet burned Smyrna in 1472.
claims.note: Venetian and papal sources record the raid; it was a reprisal for Negroponte, with little lasting effect on the war.

reigns.hook: Venice buries its admiral-doge. The electors swing to a different kind of man: Andrea Vendramin, a merchant in his eighties from a family that bought its way into the nobility.

reigns.tagline: Old money, new nobility, and fires in Friuli
reigns.previously: Admiral Pietro Mocenigo dies after fourteen months as doge.
paragraphs: Andrea Vendramin was very rich and very old. His fortune came from trade with Alexandria and the eastern Mediterranean. His family was new money by Venetian standards: they had only been let into the Great Council in 1381, as a reward for helping pay for the war against Genoa. Nearly a century later, one of them wore the ducal cap.

His two years were grim. The Ottoman war was still going, and in 1477 Turkish horsemen crossed the Isonzo, beat a Venetian force and burned their way across Friuli, close enough to scare the city. Vendramin died on 5 May 1478. His huge marble tomb by Tullio Lombardo first stood in the church of the Servi and now fills a wall of Santi Giovanni e Paolo.

claims.text: Venetians could see the fires in Friuli from their bell towers.
claims.note: Chroniclers said so of the 1477 raid. Friuli is far off, so it may be exaggeration, though smoke on the horizon is plausible.

claims.text: The Vendramin family entered the nobility in 1381, after the War of Chioggia.
claims.note: They were among the thirty families admitted to the Great Council for their help in paying for the war.

reigns.hook: Vendramin is dead and Venice is tired of war. The next doge, Pietro Mocenigo's brother Giovanni, will have to buy peace from Mehmed II, and the price is high.

reigns.tagline: He bought peace from the sultan, then fought the pope
reigns.previously: Old Andrea Vendramin dies with Ottoman raiders loose in Friuli.
paragraphs: Giovanni Mocenigo, brother of the admiral-doge Pietro, took over a city that could not afford more war. In January 1479 Venice made peace with Mehmed II. It gave up Negroponte and Scutari and agreed to pay the sultan a yearly sum for the right to trade. As a goodwill gesture Venice sent the painter Gentile Bellini to Constantinople, the same man who had painted Mocenigo.

Peace in the east freed Venice to grab land nearer home. In 1482 it went to war with Ferrara. The pope, Sixtus IV, started as an ally, then changed sides and put Venice under interdict in 1483. Venice ignored him. The Peace of Bagnolo in 1484 left it holding the Polesine, the rich lowlands by Rovigo.
In 1483 fire gutted part of the Doge's Palace, and rebuilding began. Then plague came back to the city. It killed Mocenigo on 4 November 1485.

claims.text: Gentile Bellini painted Giovanni Mocenigo's portrait.
claims.note: The profile portrait in the Museo Correr is dated to about 1478–79, just before Bellini left for Constantinople.

claims.text: The pope put Venice under interdict in 1483 and Venice simply carried on.
claims.note: Sixtus IV's interdict is well recorded. The clergy in Venice were ordered to keep holding services, and most did.

reigns.tagline: Nine months, one quarrel, one brother waiting
reigns.previously: Doge Giovanni Mocenigo dies of plague in November 1485.
paragraphs: Marco Barbarigo was elected in the autumn of 1485, a rich, careful man in his seventies, with plague still about in the city. There was no war to fight. Venice was enjoying a rare spell of peace with the sultan and its new lands in the Polesine.

His reign is remembered for one thing: how it ended. The doge's younger brother Agostino sat in the councils too, and the two did not get on. The story goes that Agostino contradicted Marco so rudely in a meeting that the old man went home, fell ill and died. Whatever the cause, Marco Barbarigo died on 14 August 1486, after only nine months as doge.

claims.text: Marco died after a bitter row with his brother Agostino in council.
claims.note: Told by Venetian chroniclers soon after. It may be gossip that grew once Agostino became doge himself.

claims.text: A portrait medal of Marco Barbarigo was struck while he was doge.
claims.note: Bronze medals of him, from the circle of the medallist Vettor Gambello, survive in museums including the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

reigns.hook: The electors meet again, and their choice is startling. They give the cap to the brother accused of hounding Marco to his grave: Agostino Barbarigo.

reigns.tagline: He won Cyprus, built a clock, and died unloved
reigns.previously: Marco Barbarigo dies after nine months, and a family row.
paragraphs: Agostino Barbarigo stepped into his dead brother's place and ruled for fifteen years, very much in style. He behaved more like a prince than an elected official, and people noticed. In 1489 Venice made Caterina Cornaro, Queen of Cyprus, hand her island to the Republic. She got a small court at Asolo, and Venice got Cyprus.

When Charles VIII of France marched through Italy in 1494, Venice joined the league against him and claimed a victory at Fornovo in 1495. At home the doge put up the Clock Tower on the Piazza, finished in 1499, with its blue and gold dial. Giovanni Bellini painted him kneeling before the Virgin in an altarpiece of 1488.

Then the Turks came back. In 1499 the fleet failed at Zonchio, and Lepanto fell. Modon and Coron, the old Venetian ports in Greece, were lost in 1500. Barbarigo died on 20 September 1501, with the war still on.

claims.text: Barbarigo grew rich from his office, and his heirs had to repay money.
claims.note: Investigators went through his affairs after his death and his estate was fined. Venice then set up permanent inspectors to audit every dead doge.

claims.text: Fornovo was a Venetian victory.
claims.note: Venice celebrated it as one, but the French army got through and went home. Most historians call it a draw at best.

claims.text: Bellini's Barbarigo Altarpiece shows the doge himself.
claims.note: The 1488 painting, now in San Pietro Martire on Murano, shows St Mark presenting the kneeling doge to the Virgin and Child.

reigns.hook: Barbarigo leaves a war and a bad name. Leonardo Loredan takes over, and soon the Turks will be the lesser danger: half of Europe is about to turn on Venice.

reigns.tagline: The calm face in the portrait, the whole world at his throat
reigns.previously: Agostino Barbarigo dies, unloved, with the Ottoman war going badly.
paragraphs: You've probably seen Leonardo Loredan without knowing it. Giovanni Bellini painted him soon after his election: the corno, the horned ducal cap, a white-and-gold damask robe and a face so calm it looks carved. It hangs in the National Gallery in London and it's the doge portrait everyone knows. He was going to need that calm.

Venice had grabbed too much of Italy, and everyone noticed. In December 1508 the pope, the emperor Maximilian, Louis XII of France and Ferdinand of Spain joined the League of Cambrai to carve the Republic up. On 14 May 1509 the French smashed the Venetian army at Agnadello. Within weeks almost the whole mainland was gone. Venice clawed Padua back that July, held on, and waited for its enemies to fall out.

They did. The pope switched sides, the alliances spun round, and by 1517 most of the mainland was Venetian again. In 1516 the Senate ordered the city's Jews to live on a walled island in Cannaregio, by an old foundry. The foundry was the ghetto, and the word stuck. Loredan died in office in June 1521, aged 84, after nearly 20 years.

claims.text: After Agnadello, Venice lost in one day what it had taken 800 years to win.
claims.note: Machiavelli says almost exactly this in The Prince (chapter 12), using the defeat as a warning against hired armies. It's his verdict, not a measurement.

claims.text: Venice's ghetto of 1516 gave the world the word.
claims.note: The area was named after a foundry (getto) that had stood there. The Senate decree of March 1516 is the first ghetto so called.

claims.text: Bellini painted Loredan as a perfect, almost timeless image of the office.
claims.note: The National Gallery dates the portrait to about 1501–02, right after his election. It's a statement about the job as much as the man.

reigns.hook: Loredan dies after nearly twenty years. His successor is 86, and once came home from a lost sea battle to stand trial: Antonio Grimani.

reigns.tagline: From chained admiral to doge at 86
reigns.previously: Leonardo Loredan dies in office after nearly twenty years.
paragraphs: Antonio Grimani made a fortune in trade and spent it buying favour. In 1499 he was captain general of the fleet at Zonchio, and the battle went badly. Captains ignored orders and Grimani failed to press the attack. Venice wanted someone to blame. He was tried, stripped of office and exiled to the island of Cres.

He escaped to Rome, where his son Domenico was a cardinal, and worked the papal court on Venice's behalf. In time he was pardoned and brought home, and the old man climbed back up, until in July 1521 the electors made him doge at 86. It was the most complete comeback in Venetian history.
His reign was short and anxious. In 1522 Sultan Suleiman took Rhodes from the Knights of St John, and Venice kept its head down. Grimani died on 7 May 1523, aged 88.

claims.text: Crowds chanted 'Antonio Grimani, ruin of Christians' after Zonchio.
claims.note: The rhyming jingle is quoted by chroniclers of the time. How widely it was chanted is anyone's guess.

claims.text: He came home to stand trial in chains, with his son the cardinal at his side.
claims.note: Told in Venetian chronicles; the details of the chains vary between versions.

reigns.hook: Grimani's comeback ends in his grave. The next doge is the man who retook Padua in 1509 and once sat in an Ottoman prison: Andrea Gritti.

reigns.tagline: The grain merchant who'd been jailed by the Sultan
reigns.previously: Antonio Grimani, the disgraced admiral made doge, dies at 88.
paragraphs: Andrea Gritti had lived for years in Constantinople, trading grain and quietly sending news home. When war with the Ottomans broke out in 1499 he was thrown in prison as a spy. He came out alive, and later helped make the peace. Back home he turned soldier. In July 1509, right after Agnadello, he led the force that recaptured Padua.

Constantinople left more than memories. His illegitimate son Alvise Gritti, born there, grew up to be a trusted adviser of the grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha. So the doge of Venice had a son in the Sultan's inner circle. As doge, Gritti steered through the wars of Italy, including the year imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527, and kept Venice standing.

He also gave the city a new face. The architect Jacopo Sansovino rebuilt the Piazza with the Library and the little Loggetta below the bell tower. Then came another Ottoman war. In 1538 the allied Christian fleet of the Holy League backed away from a fight at Preveza and lost the day. Gritti died that December, with the war still on.

claims.text: Gritti was jailed in Constantinople as a spy.
claims.note: That he was arrested in 1499 is well attested. How close he came to death and how much spying he really did varies by telling.

claims.text: His son Alvise Gritti became an adviser to Ibrahim Pasha.
claims.note: Alvise's career at the Ottoman court, and his violent death in Transylvania in 1534, are well documented by Venetian ambassadors.

claims.text: Titian's famous portrait shows Gritti from life.
claims.note: The Washington painting is dated after Gritti's death. Titian knew him, but this version was painted from memory or earlier studies.

reigns.hook: Gritti dies with the Turkish war still on. The next doge, Pietro Lando, is elected for one job: making peace with Suleiman, whatever it costs.

reigns.tagline: The doge who paid for peace with Greek towns
reigns.previously: Andrea Gritti dies in December 1538, with the Turkish war still on.
paragraphs: Pietro Lando inherited a lost war. After the Holy League fleet backed off at Preveza in 1538, Venice's allies were no use and its trade was choking. Lando was elected in January 1539, in his late seventies, and his job was to get out on the best terms possible.

The terms were bad. In the peace of 1540 Venice gave up Nauplia and Monemvasia, its last towns on the Greek mainland, along with islands in the Aegean, and paid a large indemnity. It hurt, but it bought the Republic thirty years without a major war with the Turks.
The rest of his reign was quiet. In 1543 he attended the consecration of the rebuilt church of San Zaccaria. He died on 9 November 1545, aged about 83.

claims.text: The Turks knew Venice's bottom line because Venetian officials sold it.
claims.note: In 1542 it came out that state secretaries had sold the Senate's secret instructions to the French, who passed them on. Some of those caught were hanged.

claims.text: The peace cost Venice 300,000 ducats as well as land.
claims.note: The figure appears in the standard histories; accounts differ on how it was paid.

reigns.hook: Lando is dead, and Europe is at war again around Venice. His successor, Francesco Donà, has one policy: stay out of it.

reigns.tagline: Keep calm, stay neutral, and lock up the architect
reigns.previously: Pietro Lando, who bought peace with the Turks, dies at about 83.
paragraphs: Francesco Donà, often written Donato, came to power just as Emperor Charles V and the kings of France were fighting over Italy again, and the Protestant princes of Germany were heading for war with the emperor. Venice wanted none of it. Donà kept the Republic neutral for eight years and let its trade recover.

The building work on the Piazza carried on. In December 1545, weeks into his reign, part of the vault of Sansovino's new library collapsed. The architect was thrown in prison. His friends, among them the painter Titian and the writer Pietro Aretino, got him out, and he went on to finish the library and the Loggetta beneath the bell tower. Donà died in office on 23 May 1553.

claims.text: Jacopo Sansovino was jailed when his library vault fell in.
claims.note: The collapse of December 1545 is well documented. He was released soon after, fined and made to pay for the repairs.

claims.text: Titian painted Donà's official portrait for the Doge's Palace.
claims.note: It was lost in the palace fires of the 1570s. Workshop versions and copies survive.

reigns.hook: Donà's long calm is over. The electors choose a holy, unwilling old man, Marcantonio Trevisan, who would much rather be at prayer than in power.

reigns.tagline: The saintly doge who barely wanted the job
reigns.previously: Francesco Donà dies after eight quiet, neutral years.
paragraphs: Marcantonio Trevisan was known for prayer, fasting and charity, not ambition. He was in his late seventies when he was elected in June 1553, and he tried to say no. The office was hard to refuse, so he took it and ran it like a monk, spending long hours at Mass and giving money to the poor.

Titian painted him in his ducal robes, and his portrait is now in Budapest. He did not last long. On 31 May 1554, less than a year after his election, he died suddenly. He was buried in San Francesco della Vigna. Years later Tintoretto's workshop painted him with Pietro Lando, both kneeling before the dead Christ, for the Doge's Palace.

claims.text: Trevisan tried to turn down the office.
claims.note: Venetian accounts paint him as a reluctant saint. Refusal was hardly an option: Venetian law did not let a man elected doge simply decline.

claims.text: He was struck down during Mass.
claims.note: Some later accounts say he collapsed at prayer. It fits his pious image too neatly to trust without better evidence.

reigns.hook: After less than a year the cap is free again. It goes to Francesco Venier, a younger man in his sixties, but one whose body is already failing.

reigns.tagline: Titian painted him; illness wore him down
reigns.previously: Pious Marcantonio Trevisan dies within a year of his election.
paragraphs: Francesco Venier was elected on 11 June 1554, just after his 65th birthday, young for a doge of the time. He came from one of Venice's oldest families, the same clan that would later give the city Sebastiano Venier of Lepanto.

Titian painted him in a magnificent portrait, now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Madrid: the cap, the rich robe and a pale, drawn face. It was an honest likeness. Venier was ill for much of his reign and often too weak for the long ceremonies the job demanded. Abroad, Venice stayed neutral as the new pope, Paul IV, moved towards war with Spain. Venier died on 2 June 1556, after less than two years.

claims.text: Titian's portrait of Venier is in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, Madrid.
claims.note: It is dated to his reign, 1554–56, and is one of Titian's best doge portraits.

claims.text: Venier was too sick to carry out many of his duties.
claims.note: Contemporaries describe a long illness; how much of the job he actually missed is unclear.

reigns.hook: Another short reign is over. The next doge, Lorenzo Priuli, will bring his wife into the story, and Venice will throw her the party of the century.

reigns.tagline: His wife got the coronation the city remembered
reigns.previously: Sickly Francesco Venier dies after two years as doge.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Priuli was elected in June 1556, a wealthy noble in his late sixties. His reign is remembered for his wife. In September 1557 Zilia Dandolo was crowned dogaressa with days of pageantry: processions on the water, the guilds in their finery, banquets in the Doge's Palace. Such coronations had become rare, and Venice made the most of it.

Outside, the long Italian Wars were finally ending. In April 1559 France and Spain signed the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis, leaving Spain master of much of Italy. Venice had stayed out and kept its freedom. Priuli died on 17 August 1559. He and his brother Girolamo share a grand tomb in the church of San Salvador.

claims.text: Zilia Dandolo's coronation in 1557 was one of the great festivals of the century.
claims.note: Contemporaries described it at length, and the oath she swore in September 1557 was still being painted and engraved centuries later.

claims.text: Lorenzo and his brother Girolamo share one tomb in San Salvador.
claims.note: The double monument was made in 1578–82, long after both brothers had died.

reigns.hook: Lorenzo is dead, but the Priuli are not finished. Two weeks later the electors hand the cap to his elder brother, Girolamo.

reigns.tagline: Big brother takes over the family business
reigns.cameToPower: Elected two weeks after his brother died
reigns.previously: Lorenzo Priuli dies just as the long Italian wars end.
paragraphs: Lorenzo Priuli had barely been buried when the electors chose his older brother. Girolamo Priuli was in his seventies, rich, steady and known to everybody. Brother following brother looked odd in a republic that hated dynasties, but nobody saw a plot in it. The Priuli simply had the right name at the right moment.

His eight years were quiet ones, and Venice wanted exactly that. Spain and France had finally made peace at Cateau-Cambrésis, and the Ottomans were busy elsewhere. When the Turks besieged Malta in 1565, Venice watched from the sidelines and kept trading. In 1563 the Council of Trent closed, and Venice accepted its decrees on church reform.

The money went into stone. In 1566 Palladio began the great white church of San Giorgio Maggiore across the water from the Piazzetta. That same year Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent died on campaign, and his son Selim II took over, a man with an eye on Cyprus. Girolamo Priuli died in November 1567, and the quiet years went with him.

claims.text: Girolamo and Lorenzo Priuli were brothers who followed each other as doge.
claims.note: The election records and every standard list of doges agree; Girolamo was elected on 1 September 1559.

claims.text: Venice was quick to accept the decrees of the Council of Trent.
claims.note: It did publish them, but it guarded its own control over the Church closely, and that friction later exploded under Leonardo Donà.

reigns.hook: The electors want another safe pair of hands. They pick Pietro Loredan, in his mid-eighties, just as hunger and fire close in on the city.

reigns.tagline: An old man, an empty granary and a burning Arsenal
reigns.previously: Girolamo Priuli dies after eight quiet years.
paragraphs: Pietro Loredan was elected in late November 1567, in his mid-eighties. That suited the patricians fine. An old doge was a short doge, and nobody expected him to change anything.

Then the harvests failed. Bread got dear and grain ran short, and ordinary Venetians blamed the man in the ducal palace. In September 1569 a huge explosion tore through part of the Arsenal, the shipyard that built Venice's war fleet. Rumour said Ottoman agents had set it off. The damage turned out to be smaller than feared, but the scare was real.

In Constantinople, Selim II had decided that Cyprus should be his. Early in 1570 his envoy arrived in Venice with the demand: hand the island over or face war. The Senate refused. Pietro Loredan died on 3 May 1570, before the first Ottoman soldier landed.

claims.text: Hungry crowds mocked Loredan as the doge who brought famine.
claims.note: The shortages are well documented, but the jeers and nicknames come from later, colourful retellings.

claims.text: The Arsenal explosion of 1569 was Ottoman sabotage.
claims.note: Venetians at the time suspected Joseph Nasi, Selim's Jewish adviser, but there's no proof. Gunpowder accidents were common.

reigns.hook: War with the Ottomans is coming whether Venice likes it or not. The electors need a doge who can steer through it, and they choose Alvise Mocenigo.

paragraphs: Mocenigo was barely in the job when an Ottoman army landed on Cyprus in 1570. Nicosia fell in weeks. Famagusta held out for almost a year and surrendered on terms in August 1571. The terms were broken. Its commander, Marcantonio Bragadin, had his ears cut off, was tormented for days and was then flayed alive, and his skin was stuffed and carried off as a trophy.

Two months later came revenge. On 7 October 1571 the Holy League fleet met the Ottomans at Lepanto, off western Greece. The Venetian ships were led by Sebastiano Venier, a fiery man in his seventies. It was a crushing Christian victory and church bells rang across Europe. But Venice couldn't fight on alone, and in 1573 it made a separate peace and handed Cyprus over anyway.

There was glamour too. In 1574 the young Henry III of France passed through, and Venice threw him a show of floating parties and banquets he never forgot. Then plague struck in 1575. Thousands died, and the Senate vowed a new church, Palladio's Redentore, if it ended. Mocenigo died in June 1577, before it was built.

claims.text: Bragadin was flayed alive after Famagusta surrendered.
claims.note: Survivors' accounts agree. Pieces of skin said to be his are in an urn in the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, stolen back from Constantinople.

claims.text: Lepanto changed the balance of power in the Mediterranean.
claims.note: The Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year and kept Cyprus. Historians see it as a huge morale boost more than a turning point.

claims.text: The plague of 1575–77 killed a quarter to a third of the city.
claims.note: Figures around 50,000 dead are often given, but counts from the time are patchy.

reigns.hook: Lepanto's hero is still alive, still furious, and in his eighties. In June 1577 the electors give the old admiral the corno.

reigns.tagline: The old sea dog of Lepanto gets a year on the throne
reigns.cameToPower: Elected as the hero of Lepanto
reigns.previously: Cyprus is lost, plague rages, and Alvise Mocenigo is dead.
paragraphs: Sebastiano Venier was famously short-tempered. At Lepanto he'd fought on his own deck, crossbow in hand, in his seventies. Venice loved him for it. In June 1577, with the plague burning out, the city made him doge as a thank-you. He was about 81.

Then, on 20 December 1577, fire broke out in the Doge's Palace. It gutted the Great Council hall, the biggest room in Venice. The paintings by Bellini, Titian and others went up in smoke, and so did the frieze of doge portraits running under the ceiling. The faces you see there today, Faliero's black cloth included, were all painted after this fire.
The old admiral never saw the hall rebuilt. He died in March 1578, after just nine months as doge. Since 1907 his remains have lain in Santi Giovanni e Paolo, the great church of the doges.

claims.text: Venier fought at Lepanto wearing slippers, for a better grip on the deck.
claims.note: A much-loved story told about him later. Contemporary accounts stress his courage, not his footwear.

claims.text: The fire of 1577 broke his heart and hastened his death.
claims.note: A neat story, but a man in his early eighties hardly needed a broken heart to die.

reigns.hook: The palace is a blackened shell. Rebuilding it falls to Nicolò da Ponte, an 87-year-old veteran diplomat who once argued Venice's case at the Council of Trent.

reigns.tagline: An 87-year-old rebuilds the palace and meets Japan
reigns.previously: Sebastiano Venier dies; the Doge's Palace is a burnt shell.
paragraphs: Nicolò da Ponte had spent a lifetime as a diplomat. In the 1560s he'd argued Venice's case at the Council of Trent. In March 1578 he was elected doge at 87, and he got to work. The Great Council hall had to be rebuilt after the fire, and the walls and ceilings were handed to Veronese, Tintoretto and their workshops. The doge portraits around the top were painted all over again.

His years also changed how Venice was run. In 1582 the Great Council stripped the Council of Ten of its extra members and much of its grip on money and foreign policy, and handed that power back to the Senate. That same year the Pope's new Gregorian calendar came in, and Venice adopted it at once.

In the summer of 1585 four teenage Japanese Christians arrived, envoys sent by Catholic lords in Kyushu to see the pope. Venice laid on processions and gifts. A Tintoretto workshop portrait of one of them, Itō Mancio, turned up in Milan in 2014. Da Ponte died on 30 July 1585, aged 94.

claims.text: The portrait of Itō Mancio found in 2014 is by Domenico Tintoretto.
claims.note: Experts attribute it to Jacopo Tintoretto's son Domenico. Records show the Senate ordered a portrait of the envoys, but the link isn't airtight.

claims.text: The 1582 reform broke the power of the Council of Ten.
claims.note: It removed the Ten's added members and their hold on state finance, but the Ten stayed a feared police and security court for two more centuries.

reigns.hook: Da Ponte is gone, and the rotting wooden Rialto Bridge is next. His successor, Pasquale Cicogna, will finally put it up in stone.

reigns.tagline: The doge of the stone bridge and the star fortress
reigns.previously: Nicolò da Ponte dies at 94, soon after the Japanese visit.
paragraphs: Pasquale Cicogna didn't come from one of the grand old families, and few expected him to win. But he had a fine record in Venice's overseas posts, including Crete, and the crowd in the Piazza cheered him. He was 76 when he took office in August 1585, and he'd last almost ten years.

The project everyone remembers is the Rialto Bridge. The old wooden one had collapsed and been patched for centuries. Famous architects sent designs, but the contract went to Antonio da Ponte, who built a single bold stone arch lined with shops between 1588 and 1591. Critics said it would fall down. It's still there.

Cicogna's Venice also looked to its land border. On 7 October 1593, the anniversary of Lepanto, work began on Palmanova in Friuli, a fortress town laid out as a nine-pointed star to block invaders from the east. Galileo was lecturing at Padua by then. Cicogna died on 2 April 1595.

claims.text: While Cicogna was serving on Crete, a consecrated wafer flew from a priest's hands into his.
claims.note: A pious story told in Venice to show he was marked by God. It comes from admirers, not from any independent record.

claims.text: Venice was the first Catholic state to recognise the Protestant-born Henry IV as king of France.
claims.note: Venice did recognise him early, in 1589, to Spain's fury, but who was first depends on how you count.

claims.text: Critics doubted the single-arch Rialto Bridge would stand.
claims.note: Rival architects, Vincenzo Scamozzi among them, argued against the design. It has stood for over 400 years.

reigns.hook: Cicogna is dead. Next comes a fabulously rich man who buys the crowd's love with bread and coins, and whose wife's coronation will outshine his own: Marino Grimani.

reigns.cameToPower: Elected after a long, costly contest
reigns.previously: Pasquale Cicogna dies; the stone Rialto Bridge stands.
paragraphs: Marino Grimani was one of the richest men in Venice and not shy about it. When he won in April 1595 he threw money to the crowds in the Piazza. At 62 he was young for a doge, which worried the old guard. A doge with time on his hands might get ideas.

His great show came in May 1597, when his wife, Morosina Morosini, was crowned dogaressa. It was the most lavish festival in years, with a parade of guilds and boats, and Pope Clement VIII sent her the Golden Rose, a rare papal honour.

Real trouble kept simmering. Uskok pirates kept raiding from Habsburg ports. With Rome, Venice passed laws stopping new churches and limiting church property, and Pope Paul V took it badly. Grimani died on Christmas Day 1605, with the quarrel about to blow up.

claims.text: Morosina Morosini received the Golden Rose from Pope Clement VIII.
claims.note: The gift is recorded in Venice and in Rome; it was a rare honour for a dogaressa.

claims.text: Grimani spent a fortune buying votes and goodwill to win the election.
claims.note: His largesse to the crowd is well documented, but outright vote-buying among the electors is harder to prove.

reigns.hook: The new doge, Leonardo Donà, is a lawyer's dream and a pope's nightmare. Within months Rome and Venice are heading for their biggest clash in centuries.

reigns.tagline: Excommunicated, and he simply carried on
reigns.previously: Marino Grimani dies on Christmas Day 1605, with Rome hostile.
paragraphs: Venice insisted that its own courts could try priests and that the Church couldn't keep piling up property. Pope Paul V said no. In April 1606 he excommunicated the Senate and put the whole city under interdict, which meant no Masses, no sacraments. Donà's government answered that the interdict was invalid, ordered the clergy to carry on as normal, and threw out the Jesuits, who sided with Rome.

Venice's champion was a Servite friar, Paolo Sarpi, who fought the pope in pamphlets read all over Europe. France brokered a face-saving deal in April 1607 and the interdict was lifted. That October, Sarpi was stabbed by assassins near his convent. He survived, and Rome's hand was widely suspected.

In August 1609 Galileo climbed the bell tower of St Mark's with a group of senators and let them look through his new telescope. They could see ships far out at sea, hours before anyone else. Venice gave him a pay rise. Donà died in office in July 1612.

claims.text: Sarpi joked: 'I recognise the style of the Roman Curia.'
claims.note: A pun on stylus, a pen and a dagger. It is reported by his early biographer Fulgenzio Micanzio, but may be polished in the retelling.

claims.text: Galileo showed the senators his telescope from the Campanile.
claims.note: Galileo describes the demonstration in a letter of August 1609, and Venetian records show the raise that followed.

claims.text: Most of Venice's clergy ignored the interdict.
claims.note: Apart from the Jesuits, Capuchins and Theatines, who left, churches stayed open. The government made sure of it.

reigns.hook: Donà beat the pope. His successor, Marcantonio Memmo, inherits an older headache: pirates in the Adriatic, protected by Austria.

reigns.tagline: A Memmo again, six centuries after the last one
reigns.previously: Leonardo Donà, who stared down the pope, dies in office.
paragraphs: The Memmo family liked to say it went back to Tribuno Memmo, doge in the 10th century. In July 1612 the electors gave them their second doge, Marcantonio Memmo, a 75-year-old veteran of the republic's service.

His three years brought one lasting gift. In 1613 the procurators of St Mark's hired a new music director from Mantua, Claudio Monteverdi. He'd stay thirty years and make the basilica's music famous across Europe.

The trouble was the Uskoks. These raiders from Senj, on the Croatian coast, lived under Habsburg protection and kept looting Venetian ships and islands. Venice grew sick of complaining to Vienna. Memmo died on 31 October 1615, and within weeks the two sides were at war.

claims.text: The Memmo family descended from the 10th-century doge Tribuno Memmo.
claims.note: Venice's old families all claimed ancient roots; the link rests on family tradition and the same surname.

claims.text: Monteverdi was hired as music director of St Mark's in 1613.
claims.note: His appointment by the procurators of St Mark's in August 1613 is recorded, and his own letters mention it.

reigns.hook: Venetian troops are marching on Gradisca, an Austrian fortress in Friuli. The man who has to see the war through is Giovanni Bembo, who fought at Lepanto as a young man.

reigns.tagline: A Lepanto veteran fights the pirates' protectors
reigns.previously: Marcantonio Memmo dies as war with Austria looms.
paragraphs: Giovanni Bembo had been at Lepanto in 1571 as a young man, and he'd spent much of his life at sea. That made him the obvious pick in December 1615, when Venice was at war with Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, the protector of the Uskok pirates.

The fighting centred on the Austrian fortress of Gradisca, in Friuli. Venice besieged it, and the war dragged on without a winner. Meanwhile the Spanish viceroy of Naples, the Duke of Osuna, sent warships into the Adriatic to bully Venice, which had always called that sea its own.
Peace was agreed in 1617. The Habsburgs agreed to move the Uskoks inland and burn their boats, which was all Venice had wanted. Bembo didn't enjoy it long. He died on 16 March 1618.

claims.text: Bembo fought at Lepanto.
claims.note: His service in the 1571 campaign is part of his recorded career, and it was used to praise him at his election.

claims.text: The war of Gradisca solved the Uskok problem.
claims.note: The peace of 1617–18 moved the Uskoks away from the coast, and the raids largely stopped.

reigns.tagline: Thirty-odd days in the corno, then gone
reigns.previously: Giovanni Bembo dies soon after peace with Austria.
paragraphs: Electing a doge took days. Since 1268 Venice had used a crazy chain of ten rounds, drawing lots and voting in turn, until a final 41 electors chose the doge. The idea was that no family could rig it. In April 1618 the chain spat out Nicolò Donà, a 79-year-old veteran patrician.

He swore the promissione, the long oath listing everything a doge couldn't do, and was crowned with the corno, the stiff cap of office. Then, early in May 1618, barely a month later, he died. He's one of the shortest-serving doges in the republic's history.
There was no time to make a mark, and no sign he tried. Venice simply buried him with full honours and started the whole long election over again.

claims.text: Donà died from the strain of his election.
claims.note: A natural story to tell about a man who died within weeks, but there's no good evidence. He was 79.

claims.text: The doge's electors were picked by ten alternating rounds of lot and vote.
claims.note: The procedure was set in 1268 and is described in Venetian law and every history of the republic.

reigns.hook: The next doge, Antonio Priuli, takes office in May 1618 just as the Council of Ten uncovers a Spanish plot to seize the city. Bodies are about to swing in the Piazzetta.

reigns.tagline: Plots, gallows and an innocent man hanged
reigns.previously: Nicolò Donà dies a month into the job.
paragraphs: Antonio Priuli was elected in May 1618, and within days the Council of Ten announced it had smashed a Spanish plot to seize Venice. Mercenaries were arrested, and bodies were hung up in the Piazzetta for all to see. The Spanish ambassador, the Marquis of Bedmar, left the city in a hurry. The story later inspired a famous English play, Venice Preserv'd.

Then the Ten went too far. In 1622 they convicted Antonio Foscarini, a senator and former ambassador to England, of selling secrets to foreign diplomats, partly because he'd visited the house of an English noblewoman, the Countess of Arundel. He was strangled in prison, and his body was hung by one leg in the Piazzetta.
Months later the Ten found the informers had lied. In January 1623 they declared Foscarini innocent and apologised to the countess. Priuli died that August.

claims.text: The Spanish conspiracy of 1618 was real.
claims.note: Historians still argue whether Bedmar and the Duke of Osuna really planned a coup, or the Ten blew up a few rumours.

claims.text: The Ten publicly declared Foscarini innocent.
claims.note: The Council of Ten issued a formal declaration clearing him in January 1623, an almost unheard-of climbdown.

reigns.hook: Venice wants a calm, safe pair of hands after the scandal. It chooses Francesco Contarini, a veteran diplomat in his sixties.

reigns.tagline: A diplomat's short turn at the top
reigns.previously: Antonio Priuli dies after the Foscarini scandal.
paragraphs: Francesco Contarini belonged to the biggest clan in the Venetian nobility, which gave the republic eight doges in all. He'd spent his career as a diplomat, carrying Venice's messages to foreign courts. In September 1623 he was elected at 66.

The big worry was the Valtellina, an Alpine valley north of Lake Como. Spain had grabbed it to link its lands in Italy with the Habsburgs in Austria. Venice, France and Savoy agreed early in 1623 to push the Spanish out, and under Contarini Venice helped pay for the campaign of 1624.
He didn't see how it ended. Contarini died on 6 December 1624, after just fifteen months as doge.

claims.text: The Contarini gave Venice eight doges, more than any other family.
claims.note: Standard lists of doges count eight Contarini, from Domenico in the 11th century to Alvise in the 17th.

reigns.tagline: A doge's son, a dagger and a crisis for the Ten
reigns.previously: Francesco Contarini dies after fifteen months.
paragraphs: Giovanni Corner came from one of the richest families in Venice. The law said a doge's sons couldn't hold high office while he lived, but the Corner sons kept collecting jobs and church posts anyway. One of them, Federico, was made a cardinal in 1626.

Renier Zeno, a fierce patrician serving as one of the heads of the Council of Ten, said so loudly. He accused the doge's family of breaking the rules. At the end of 1627 Zeno was attacked and badly wounded, and the doge's son Giorgio Corner was found to be behind it. Giorgio fled and was banished.

The scandal set off a furious debate in 1628 about whether the Ten had grown too powerful. Reformers tried to cut its powers but the Ten survived much as before. Corner died on 23 December 1629, with plague creeping into northern Italy.

claims.text: Giorgio Corner organised the attack on Renier Zeno.
claims.note: The Council of Ten found him responsible and banished him; the case is studied in detail by Gaetano Cozzi.

claims.text: Corner's sons held offices that the law forbade to a doge's children.
claims.note: This was Zeno's charge, and the doge's own oath barred his sons from most offices during his reign.

reigns.hook: The plague is coming. Venice turns to a scholar who writes its history, Nicolò Contarini, and he is about to live through one of the worst years the city has ever known.

reigns.tagline: The historian doge who ruled through the great plague
reigns.reignEnded: Died in office as the plague raged
reigns.previously: Giovanni Corner dies, his family's scandal still the talk of Venice.
paragraphs: Nicolò Contarini was a scholar first. As a younger man he had stood with Paolo Sarpi when Venice defied the pope, and he spent years writing a history of the Republic in his own time. He was elected on 18 January 1630, aged 76, and trouble came fast. Venice had joined the war over who should inherit Mantua, and in May its army broke and ran at Valeggio.

Worse came from Mantua too. That summer a Mantuan envoy and his party arrived carrying plague. They were put in quarantine on an island in the lagoon, but a carpenter who worked there took the disease back into the city. By autumn Venetians were dying in thousands. In October the Senate vowed a great church to the Virgin if she would end it. The young architect Baldassare Longhena won the job of designing Santa Maria della Salute.
Contarini never saw it rise. He died on 2 April 1631 with the plague still loose in the streets. By the time it burned out that November, something like a third of the city was dead.

claims.text: The plague of 1630–31 killed about a third of Venice.
claims.note: Official counts give roughly 46,000 deaths in the city; the records from the worst weeks are patchy.

claims.text: The envoy who brought the plague was the librettist of Monteverdi's Orfeo.
claims.note: The Mantuan envoy was Alessandro Striggio the younger, who wrote the words of Orfeo (1607). He died of the plague in Venice in 1630.

reigns.hook: The plague is burning out and the Salute's foundations are going in. The next doge will see the church begin to rise, and see the Ottomans come for Crete.

reigns.tagline: Given the fleet at 79, dead before he could sail
reigns.reignEnded: Died before he could sail for Crete
reigns.previously: Nicolò Contarini dies with the plague still loose in the city.
paragraphs: Francesco Erizzo was elected on 10 April 1631, while the plague was still killing. Once it ended, Venice got back to living. Longhena's Salute began to climb at the mouth of the Grand Canal, and in 1637 the Teatro San Cassiano opened as the first opera house where anyone who bought a ticket could get in. Opera stopped being a treat for princes and became a night out.

Then the peace with the Ottomans, kept since the 1570s, fell apart. In 1644 the Knights of Malta seized an Ottoman ship carrying pilgrims and stopped on Crete with their prize. Sultan Ibrahim blamed Venice. In June 1645 a huge Ottoman army landed on Crete, Venice's biggest colony, and took the town of Canea in August.
Venice turned to its doge. The Senate named Erizzo, now 79, captain-general of the sea, to lead the fleet himself. He never sailed. He died on 3 January 1646 and his heart was buried in St Mark's.

claims.text: The Maltese raid was only an excuse for an attack the Ottomans already wanted.
claims.note: Venice swore it had nothing to do with the Knights. Many historians think Crete was a target anyway, but the timing points to the raid.

claims.text: Erizzo's heart lies in St Mark's, his body in another church.
claims.note: The standard lives of the doges record the heart burial in the basilica and his body in San Martino, his parish church in Castello.

claims.text: San Cassiano was the world's first public opera house.
claims.note: It opened in 1637 for a paying public. Earlier operas had been staged at princely courts for invited guests.

reigns.hook: The doge is dead and an Ottoman army is camped on Crete. His successor faces a war that Venice can barely pay for.

reigns.tagline: He sold seats in the Great Council to pay for war
reigns.cameToPower: Elected as the Cretan War began
reigns.reignEnded: Died in office, the war still on
reigns.previously: Old Erizzo dies before he can sail to save Crete.
paragraphs: Francesco Molin took office in January 1646 with Crete half lost. Canea had fallen and Rettimo followed that autumn. In 1648 the Ottomans dug in around Candia, the capital, and began a siege that would outlast Molin and four more doges.

War costs money, and Venice found it in its proudest institution. From 1646 a family that could pay 100,000 ducats could buy a hereditary seat in the Great Council, the closed club of nobles that had admitted almost nobody new for centuries. Dozens of rich merchant families bought their way in.

The navy did its part, trying to bottle up the Ottoman fleet at the Dardanelles before it could reach Crete. In 1649 a Venetian squadron caught Ottoman ships at Phocaea and burned many of them. Candia was still holding when Molin died on 27 February 1655.

claims.text: Seats in the Great Council were sold for 100,000 ducats.
claims.note: Part was paid as a gift to the state and part as a loan. Dozens of families joined this way during the war.

claims.text: Venice's fleet won a big victory at Phocaea in 1649.
claims.note: Venetian and Ottoman accounts agree on heavy Ottoman losses, though the numbers of ships burned vary.

reigns.hook: Molin is dead and Candia is still standing. Venice's next doge is an old man from its biggest noble clan, and he has barely a year to live.

reigns.tagline: A year in office while the war moved out to sea
reigns.previously: Francesco Molin dies; Candia is still holding out.
paragraphs: Carlo Contarini came from the biggest clan in the Venetian nobility. Eight doges were Contarini, more than any other family, and he was the sixth. He was elected on 27 March 1655, aged 74, and inherited a war with no end in sight. Candia was under siege and the Republic was borrowing wherever it could.

The real fight was now at sea. Venice's plan was to block the Dardanelles so that Ottoman fleets couldn't get out to resupply their army on Crete. In June 1655 a Venetian fleet beat an Ottoman force trying to break through. Contarini didn't live to see the bigger battle that followed. He died on 1 May 1656, after thirteen months.

claims.text: Eight doges came from the Contarini family.
claims.note: The standard lists count eight, from Domenico I in the 11th century to Alvise in the 17th, more than any other family.

claims.text: The Dardanelles blockade kept supplies from reaching the Ottoman army on Crete.
claims.note: It hurt the Ottomans badly in some years, but their ships kept getting through often enough to keep the siege going.

reigns.hook: Contarini is dead. His successor is the son of a doge, and his time in office will be counted in days.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Unrelated; son of Doge Giovanni I
reigns.previously: Carlo Contarini dies after barely a year as doge.
paragraphs: Francesco Corner knew the job from the inside. His father, Giovanni I Corner, had been doge from 1625 to 1629, and the family's habit of filling offices with relatives had caused a scandal that ended in a fight over the powers of the Council of Ten. A generation later the electors were happy to pick another Corner. They chose Francesco on 17 May 1656, aged 71.
He died on 5 June, nineteen days later, before he had time to do anything at all. Three weeks after his death a Venetian fleet at the Dardanelles won the greatest sea battle of the whole war.

claims.text: No doge reigned for a shorter time.
claims.note: Standard lists give his nineteen days as the shortest reign. The dates of some early doges are too vague to be completely sure.

claims.text: The Corner family gave Venice four doges.
claims.note: Marco (1365), Giovanni I (1625), Francesco (1656) and Giovanni II (1709).

reigns.hook: Nineteen days and done. The next doge takes office just in time to hear the best news Venice has had in years.

reigns.tagline: Elected days before the great win at the Dardanelles
reigns.previously: Francesco Corner dies after just nineteen days as doge.
paragraphs: Bertuccio Valier was elected on 15 June 1656, young for a doge at 59. Eleven days later came the news. On 26 June, at the mouth of the Dardanelles, the Venetian fleet smashed an Ottoman fleet trying to break out. Its commander, Lorenzo Marcello, was killed in the fighting, but Venice went on to seize the islands of Tenedos and Lemnos, right on the sultan's doorstep.

It didn't last. In 1657 the Ottomans fought back, the admiral Lazzaro Mocenigo was killed, and both islands were lost again. Venice badly needed allies, and the pope wanted a favour first. So in 1657 Valier's government let the Jesuits back into Venice, half a century after throwing them out.
Valier died on 29 March 1658. His son Silvestro would be doge one day too, and the family's huge marble monument in Santi Giovanni e Paolo honours them both.

claims.text: The 1656 Dardanelles battle was Venice's best naval victory since Lepanto.
claims.note: Venetian writers called it that. Ottoman losses were heavy, but everything it won was lost within a year.

claims.text: The Jesuits were let back in to win the pope's help in the war.
claims.note: Pope Alexander VII pressed for their return while Venice was asking Rome for money and ships.

reigns.hook: Valier is dead and the islands are lost. The next doge is the Senate's fiercest war hawk, and he will be remembered for his tomb.

reigns.tagline: The war hawk whose tomb is held up by giants
reigns.previously: Bertuccio Valier dies; the islands won at the Dardanelles are lost.
paragraphs: Giovanni Pesaro had made his name in the Senate as a hawk. When talk turned to buying peace by handing Crete to the sultan, Pesaro argued for fighting on. In April 1658 the electors made him doge, and the war went on as he wanted.

He didn't get long. Candia still held, nothing was settled, and Pesaro died on 30 September 1659, after eighteen months. What everyone remembers is his tomb in the Frari church. Designed by Baldassare Longhena, it rises in storeys up the wall, and its upper part rests on the shoulders of four giant carved figures of Black men in ragged clothes, posed as slaves. It is one of the most startling monuments in Venice, and now one of the most uncomfortable.

claims.text: Longhena designed Pesaro's tomb in the Frari.
claims.note: The monument was finished in 1669. The giant figures are usually credited to the German sculptor Melchior Barthel.

claims.text: His tomb stands beside Titian's Pesaro altarpiece, ordered by a kinsman.
claims.note: Both are on the left side of the Frari nave. Jacopo Pesaro, who ordered the Titian in the 1520s, was of the same family.

reigns.hook: Pesaro dies with Candia still under siege. His successor will hold office for fifteen years, long enough to see the city fall.

reigns.tagline: Fifteen years, and the end of Venetian Crete
reigns.reignEnded: Died in office two days shy of 90
reigns.previously: Giovanni Pesaro dies with Candia still under siege.
paragraphs: Domenico Contarini was elected in October 1659, aged 74. Nobody expected a long reign, but he lasted fifteen years and outlived the war. Peace between France and Spain that same year freed up soldiers, and volunteers from all over Catholic Europe sailed out to fight at Candia.

It wasn't enough. In 1669 Louis XIV sent a proper French force under the Duke of Beaufort. Its first big sortie went wrong, Beaufort vanished in the fighting, and the French sailed home in August. On 6 September Francesco Morosini, commanding in the ruined city, agreed terms with the grand vizier, Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha.

The defenders marched out with their lives and their honour, and Venice kept three small island forts off the coast. The rest of Crete, Venetian for over 450 years, was gone. Contarini died in office on 26 January 1675, two days short of his 90th birthday.

claims.text: The Duke of Beaufort, lost at Candia, was really the Man in the Iron Mask.
claims.note: An idea floated long afterwards. His body was never identified, but nothing links him to the masked prisoner.

claims.text: Morosini gave up Candia without the Senate's permission.
claims.note: His enemies said so and he was accused in the Great Council in 1670. He was cleared.

reigns.hook: Contarini is dead and Venice has lost Crete. The next doge is a veteran diplomat, and he will get just eighteen months of quiet.
