reigns.tagline: A diplomat's short, quiet reign after the war
reigns.previously: Domenico II Contarini dies, two days short of 90, with Crete lost.
paragraphs: Nicolò Sagredo had spent much of his career abroad as one of the Republic's ambassadors. He was elected on 6 February 1675, and his reign was one of the calmest of the century. The peace with the Ottomans held, and Venice set about licking its wounds after a quarter of a century of war.

His family name was already famous. A Sagredo, Galileo's friend Giovanni Francesco, is one of the three speakers in Galileo's Dialogue of 1632, the book that got the astronomer into trouble with Rome. Nicolò himself left a lighter mark. He died on 14 August 1676, after only eighteen months in office.

claims.text: The Sagredo of Galileo's Dialogue belonged to the doge's family.
claims.note: Giovanni Francesco Sagredo (1571–1620) was a Venetian noble of the Sagredo family. How closely he was related to the doge is less clear.

reigns.hook: Sagredo is dead, and his brother Giovanni wants the job next. The people of Venice have other ideas.

reigns.tagline: The peacemaker of Westphalia, made doge at 74
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen once Giovanni Sagredo was blocked
reigns.previously: Nicolò Sagredo dies after eighteen quiet months.
paragraphs: When Nicolò Sagredo died, the electors leaned towards his brother Giovanni, a scholar and diplomat. There was an outcry. Two brothers in a row looked like one family helping itself to the top job, and crowds made their anger plain. The Sagredo choice was dropped, and on 26 August 1676 the electors settled on Alvise Contarini instead.

Contarini was one of Venice's great diplomats. In the 1640s he spent years at Münster as a mediator in the talks that ended the Thirty Years' War with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. As doge he kept Venice at peace, which suited a city still paying for Crete.

In September 1683 an Ottoman army besieging Vienna was routed by the Polish king Jan Sobieski and his allies. Suddenly the sultan looked beatable. Contarini died on 15 January 1684, as Venice weighed up whether to join the fight.

claims.text: Giovanni Sagredo's election was blocked by public anger.
claims.note: Venetian accounts describe protests and a failed election, but how far the crowd decided it is debated.

claims.text: Contarini was a mediator at the Westphalia peace talks.
claims.note: He was Venice's mediator at Münster, working alongside the papal nuncio Fabio Chigi, later Pope Alexander VII.

reigns.hook: Contarini is dead. The pope is building a Holy League against the Ottomans, the next doge must decide whether Venice joins, and the old admiral Morosini is ready to go.

reigns.tagline: A pious doge, a holy league and the Morea won
reigns.previously: Alvise Contarini dies just as the Ottomans reel back from Vienna.
paragraphs: Marcantonio Giustinian was elected on 26 January 1684, a devout man from one of the oldest families in Venice. Few Venetians wanted another war after Crete, but this looked like the moment to win back what had been lost. In March the Republic joined the Holy League with the Emperor Leopold I, the King of Poland and Pope Innocent XI.

Francesco Morosini, the man who had surrendered Candia, was given the fleet. He took the island of Santa Maura, today's Lefkada, in 1684, then worked his way round the Peloponnese, which Venetians called the Morea: Coron in 1685, Navarino, Modon and Nauplia in 1686, Patras and Corinth in 1687.

In September 1687 his army reached Athens, and a Venetian shell set off the Ottoman powder store inside the Parthenon. The Senate gave Morosini the title Peloponnesiacus. Giustinian died on 23 March 1688, and Venice knew exactly who should come next.

claims.text: Venice joined the Holy League in March 1684.
claims.note: The alliance with the Emperor, Poland and the pope was sealed at Linz on 5 March 1684.

claims.text: The Peloponnese was called the Morea after its mulberry trees.
claims.note: A popular old explanation, from the Greek word for mulberry. Scholars still argue about where the name really comes from.

reigns.hook: The doge is dead and the hero is still in Greece. Venice elects Francesco Morosini without waiting for him to come home.

reigns.tagline: The admiral who blew up the Parthenon
reigns.cameToPower: Elected while still at the front
reigns.previously: Marcantonio Giustinian dies as Morosini conquers the Morea.
paragraphs: Morosini's army was besieging the Ottoman garrison on the Acropolis. The defenders had stored gunpowder inside the Parthenon. On 26 September 1687 a Venetian mortar shell crashed through the roof and set it off. The blast tore out the middle of the 2,100-year-old temple and killed hundreds of the people sheltering there. The Parthenon has been a ruin ever since.

Then he went shopping. He tried to lower the great horses of Athena's chariot from the west end of the temple, and the ropes gave way and smashed them. He did take the marble lion from Piraeus, which still guards the gate of the Arsenal in Venice. The Senate gave him the title Peloponnesiacus, and in April 1688 elected him doge while he was still in Greece.

Being doge didn't keep him home. His siege of Negroponte in 1688 failed, and he came back to Venice. In 1693, at 74, he sailed out once more as commander, and died at Nauplia in January 1694. He was the last doge to lead the fleet.

claims.text: About 300 people died in the Parthenon explosion.
claims.note: The figure comes from Venetian and German officers on the spot. Many of the dead were women and children sheltering inside.

claims.text: Morosini's embalmed cat is in the Museo Correr.
claims.note: A mummified cat linked to him is shown there, but the story of the cat sailing with him rests on family tradition.

claims.text: The Senate named him Peloponnesiacus in 1687.
claims.note: A Senate honour modelled on Roman victory titles, voted while he was still at war in Greece.

reigns.hook: Morosini dies at Nauplia with the Morea in Venetian hands. Back home the electors choose Silvestro Valier, a doge's son with a taste for splendour and a wife who wants a crown.

reigns.tagline: The doge whose wife got a coronation of her own
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; son of a doge
reigns.previously: Morosini, the last fighting doge, dies on campaign at Nauplia.
paragraphs: Silvestro Valier was rich, charming and a doge's son: his father Bertuccio had worn the ducal cap for two years in the 1650s. Elected in February 1694, weeks after Morosini died in Greece, he wanted a proper show. His wife, Elisabetta Querini, was crowned dogaressa with full ceremony, a party Venice talked about for years.

The war Morosini had started dragged on. A Venetian fleet seized the island of Chios in 1694 and lost it again within months. Then the tide turned at the peace table. In January 1699, at Karlowitz, the Ottomans signed over the Morea, and the whole Peloponnese was Venetian.

Valier enjoyed the peace for little more than a year. He died in July 1700. He, his father and his wife share one of the biggest tombs in Venice, a towering wall of marble statues and carved drapery in the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo.

claims.text: Elisabetta Querini was the last dogaressa to be crowned.
claims.note: Often repeated in histories of Venice. Later doges' wives got no such ceremony, but how grand the earlier ones were is patchily recorded.

claims.text: Valier died of a stroke after a row with his wife.
claims.note: A Venetian story about his death. No contemporary record backs it up.

reigns.hook: Peace at last, and the Morea is Venetian. But Europe is about to fight over the Spanish throne, and the next doge, Alvise II Mocenigo, will watch foreign armies march across his land.

reigns.tagline: Neutral, while two armies trampled his fields
reigns.previously: Silvestro Valier dies a year after peace wins Venice the Morea.
paragraphs: Alvise Mocenigo came from one of the grandest families in Venice. He was the second doge of that name; the first had reigned in the year of Lepanto. A few months after his election in July 1700, the King of Spain died without children and Europe split over who should get his empire.

Venice chose to stay out. That sounded safe, but the fighting came anyway. In 1701 Prince Eugene of Savoy led an imperial army over the Alps into Italy, and soon French and Austrian troops were marching, camping and foraging across the Venetian mainland around Verona and Brescia. The Republic protested, and nobody listened.
The winter of 1709 was the coldest anyone in Europe could remember, and the lagoon froze over. Mocenigo died that May.

claims.text: Venice stayed neutral through the whole War of the Spanish Succession.
claims.note: The Republic never joined either side, though both armies fought on its territory.

claims.text: In 1709 the lagoon froze so hard that people walked over the ice to the mainland.
claims.note: The Great Frost of 1709 is well recorded across Europe. Stories of walking to the mainland are told of several hard winters and are hard to pin down.

reigns.hook: The old doge is gone. His successor, Giovanni II Corner, will face the war Venice has dreaded since Karlowitz: the Ottomans want the Morea back.

reigns.tagline: He lost the Morea, but Corfu held
reigns.previously: Alvise II Mocenigo dies after the coldest winter in memory.
paragraphs: Giovanni Corner came from the clan that had already given Venice three doges and, long ago, a queen to Cyprus. He was elected in May 1709. Five years later the Ottomans declared war, and in 1715 a huge army swept into the Morea. The Venetian forts there were badly manned and badly kept, and they fell one after another in a matter of months.

Next came Corfu, guarding the mouth of the Adriatic. In the summer of 1716 the Ottomans landed and laid siege. The defence was led by Marshal Matthias von der Schulenburg, a German soldier in Venetian pay. After weeks of assaults the besiegers gave up and sailed away. A grateful Venice put up a statue of him on Corfu while he was still alive.

Austria joined the war and beat the Ottomans in Hungary, and the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 settled things. Venice lost the Morea for good but kept Corfu and the Dalmatian coast. It was the Republic's last war with the Sultan. Corner died in August 1722.

claims.text: Schulenburg's statue was put up on Corfu in his lifetime.
claims.note: The marble statue by Antonio Corradini still stands in Corfu town. The Republic almost never honoured a living man this way.

claims.text: A storm helped save Corfu in 1716.
claims.note: Accounts of the time say a violent storm hit the Ottoman camp just before they lifted the siege. Corfiots credit their patron saint, Spyridon.

reigns.hook: No more wars. Under the next doge, Alvise III Mocenigo, Venice learns to live on music, masks and visitors.

reigns.tagline: A quiet decade while Vivaldi played
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Same clan as Alvise II; elected
reigns.previously: Giovanni II Corner dies; Venice has lost the Morea but kept Corfu.
paragraphs: Alvise Sebastiano Mocenigo was the third Alvise Mocenigo to be doge, elected in August 1722 just before his 60th birthday. Venice had given up on war, and his ten years were some of the calmest the Republic ever had. The doge's job was now mostly ceremony: processions, banquets and the Ascension Day trip out to sea on the state barge.

The money came from visitors. Rich young men on the Grand Tour arrived for carnival and stayed for the gambling and the opera. Antonio Vivaldi, the red-haired priest, wrote for the orchestra of orphan girls at the Pietà, and in 1725 his Four Seasons appeared in print. A young painter called Canaletto began selling views of the city to English collectors.
Mocenigo died in May 1732. The Republic he left was peaceful, pretty and quietly running down.

claims.text: Vivaldi's Four Seasons was first printed in Amsterdam in 1725.
claims.note: The four concertos open his Opus 8 collection, published by Michel-Charles Le Cène.

claims.text: Vivaldi was nicknamed the Red Priest for his hair.
claims.note: Il Prete Rosso: he was ordained in 1703, and the nickname is recorded in his own time.

reigns.hook: The electors turn to an old diplomat who knows the Ottomans better than anyone: Carlo Ruzzini, the man who sat at both peace tables.

reigns.tagline: The peacemaker who kept Venice out of every war
reigns.previously: Alvise III Mocenigo dies after ten quiet years.
paragraphs: Carlo Ruzzini had spent his life at the negotiating table. He spoke for Venice at the peace talks of Karlowitz in 1699, which gave it the Morea, and at Passarowitz in 1718, which took it away again. By the time he was elected doge in June 1732 he was 78.

His long experience told him to keep out of trouble. When the War of the Polish Succession broke out in 1733, French, Spanish and Austrian armies fought over northern Italy once more. Venice kept its neutrality and its troops at home, and the armies again crossed its land. Ruzzini died in January 1735, after less than three years.

claims.text: Ruzzini was Venice's envoy at both Karlowitz (1699) and Passarowitz (1718).
claims.note: He is named as the Venetian plenipotentiary at both congresses in the standard accounts of the two treaties.

reigns.hook: Next the electors choose money. Alvise Pisani belongs to the richest family in Venice, and the Pisani are building a country house fit for a king.

reigns.tagline: The richest family in Venice gets the cap
reigns.previously: Old Carlo Ruzzini, the peacemaker, dies after under three years.
paragraphs: The Pisani were the richest clan in Venice, and in January 1735 one of them, Alvise, became doge at 71. Their palace on Campo Santo Stefano was among the largest in the city, and out on the Brenta canal at Stra they were building a country house on a royal scale, with well over a hundred rooms.

His reign was quiet. In 1740 the death of Emperor Charles VI set off the War of the Austrian Succession, and Venice stayed neutral again. Pisani died in June 1741. His family's villa went on growing for years after him.

claims.text: Villa Pisani at Stra was built to celebrate Alvise's election as doge.
claims.note: Building went on for decades either side of his election, so the link is loose. Napoleon bought the villa in 1807.

claims.text: Tiepolo painted the villa's great ballroom ceiling.
claims.note: His fresco glorifying the Pisani family dates from the early 1760s, long after Alvise's death.

reigns.hook: His successor, Pietro Grimani, is a polished old ambassador who knows London. He will have to defend Venice from the sea itself.

reigns.tagline: A gentleman doge builds walls against the sea
reigns.previously: Alvise Pisani dies, rich and untroubled, in 1741.
paragraphs: Pietro Grimani was a cultured man who had served as ambassador in London and liked the company of writers. He was elected doge in June 1741, aged 63. Europe was at war again over the Austrian succession, and Venice sat it out once more.

The real threat came from the water. Storms kept breaking through the long sandbanks of the Lido and Pellestrina that shield the lagoon. In 1744 the Republic began the murazzi, massive sea walls of Istrian stone. They took almost forty years to finish and still stand.

The war hurt the tourist trade, and Canaletto, short of buyers, moved to London in 1746 and stayed for most of the next ten years. At home, Carlo Goldoni was writing a new kind of comedy about ordinary Venetians. Grimani died in March 1752.

claims.text: The murazzi were begun in 1744.
claims.note: Planned by the engineer Bernardino Zendrini. A Latin inscription of 1751 on the wall boasts of colossal blocks of solid marble set against the sea.

claims.text: Canaletto went to London because the war had cut off his English customers.
claims.note: The usual explanation. His agent, the merchant Joseph Smith, had long sold his views to English collectors.

reigns.tagline: The doge whose roof lost Casanova
reigns.previously: Pietro Grimani dies, with sea walls rising along the Lido.
paragraphs: Francesco Loredan, elected in March 1752 at 67, came from the same clan as Leonardo Loredan, the doge of Bellini's famous portrait. His ten years were peaceful, and the most famous event of his reign happened right over his head.

In July 1755 the State Inquisitors arrested Giacomo Casanova, gambler, charmer and dabbler in magic, and locked him in the Piombi, the cells under the lead roof of the Doge's Palace. On the night of 31 October 1756 he and a monk, Marino Balbi, broke out through the roof, got back inside through a window and walked out of the palace's main door. He fled to Paris and made the story famous.

The Seven Years' War tore across Europe from 1756, and Venice stayed out. At home, some nobles began asking whether the Council of Ten and its Inquisitors had too much power. Loredan died in May 1762 with that argument still raging.

claims.text: Casanova escaped from the Piombi on 31 October 1756.
claims.note: Casanova told the story himself and liked to embroider, but the escape is confirmed by the Venetian records.

claims.text: Casanova was never told what he had been charged with.
claims.note: That is his own account. The Inquisitors' papers point to irreligion and dabbling in the occult.

reigns.hook: The electors choose a scholar. Marco Foscarini, historian of Venetian literature, raises great hopes. He will have ten months.

reigns.tagline: The scholar doge who lasted ten months
reigns.previously: Francesco Loredan dies; Casanova escaped on his watch.
paragraphs: Marco Foscarini was one of the most learned men ever to be doge. He had been a diplomat and a historian, and in 1752 he published a big history of Venetian literature. In May 1762, aged 66, he was elected.

He came in at the end of a bitter row. In 1761 the Inquisitors had arrested Angelo Querini, a noble who said the Council of Ten had grown too powerful, and the Great Council spent months arguing about reform. In the end the old system survived with only small changes. Foscarini, the finest speaker of his day, was on the side of keeping it.
People hoped a scholar would bring fresh ideas to the ducal throne. There was no time. Foscarini died in March 1763, ten months after his election.

claims.text: Foscarini's speech persuaded the Great Council to keep the Council of Ten's powers in 1762.
claims.note: Histories of the 1761 to 1762 reform debate credit his speech. How far it alone swung the vote is less clear.

claims.text: His history of Venetian literature was never finished.
claims.note: Only the first part, published in 1752, ever appeared.

reigns.hook: Next comes Alvise IV Mocenigo, who will go after the Church's wealth and shut the city's most famous gambling house.

reigns.tagline: The doge who shut the casino
reigns.previously: Marco Foscarini, the scholar doge, dies after ten months.
paragraphs: Alvise Giovanni Mocenigo, the fourth doge of that name, was elected in April 1763 at 61. Pushed by reformers such as Andrea Tron, the Senate went after the Church's riches. It limited new gifts of land to churches and closed many small monasteries and convents.

Visitors kept coming. In 1771 the teenage Mozart spent carnival in Venice with his father. But many nobles were getting poorer, and too many were gambling away what they had left at the Ridotto, the state-run casino. In November 1774 the Great Council voted to close it.
Trade shrank, the fleet aged, and the number of noble families kept falling. Mocenigo died on the last day of 1778.

claims.text: The Great Council voted to close the Ridotto in 1774.
claims.note: The vote came in late November 1774. The gambling simply moved into private casini around the city.

claims.text: Mozart and his father spent carnival 1771 in Venice.
claims.note: Leopold Mozart's letters home describe the visit.

reigns.tagline: The doge who told Venice it had no strength left
reigns.previously: Alvise IV Mocenigo dies on the last day of 1778.
paragraphs: Paolo Renier was clever, a fine speaker and short of money. He had served as Venice's envoy, the bailo, in Constantinople, and he came home with a wife the nobility thoroughly disapproved of. When he was elected doge in January 1779, at 68, the gossip said he had paid for it.

In 1780 he told the Great Council the hard truth: Venice had no real forces on land or sea and no allies, and it lived on luck and other people's goodwill. The admiral Angelo Emo showed the old navy still had some teeth, bombarding Tunisian ports between 1784 and 1786 to stop corsairs preying on Venetian ships.
Renier died on 13 February 1789, in the middle of carnival. The government did not want to spoil the season, the story goes, so his death was kept quiet until the festivities were over.

claims.text: Renier bought his election.
claims.note: The charge came from rivals and later writers. Vote-buying was illegal and hard to prove.

claims.text: His wife had been a tightrope dancer in Constantinople.
claims.note: Venetian gossip of the time. Her past and even her origins are poorly documented.

claims.text: Renier's death was kept secret until carnival was over.
claims.note: A popular story that fits the image of a city that put the party first. Firm evidence is thin.

reigns.hook: Renier is gone. The electors pick the richest man they can find, Ludovico Manin. In Paris that summer, the Bastille is about to fall.

reigns.tagline: The last doge hands over his hat
reigns.previously: Paolo Renier dies; the news is held back until carnival ends.
paragraphs: Ludovico Manin was the 120th doge, by the usual count, and the last. His family came from Friuli and had bought its way into the nobility in 1651. Snobs never forgot it. His reign had one bright spot: in 1792 the opera house La Fenice opened. Then the young general Napoleon Bonaparte marched into Italy in 1796, chasing the Austrians straight across neutral Venetian land.

In April 1797 the people of Verona rose against the French. Days later the guns of the Lido fort fired on a French ship that tried to force its way into the lagoon, and its captain was killed. Napoleon had his excuse and declared war on 1 May. Venice had no real army or fleet left to fight with.

On 12 May 1797 the Great Council voted to end the Republic after over a thousand years. French troops marched in. In October, at Campo Formio, Napoleon handed Venice to Austria's Francis II, and the bronze horses of St Mark's went off to Paris. Manin lived quietly in Venice and died in 1802.

claims.text: An old noble grumbled that a Friulian doge meant the Republic was dead.
claims.note: Pinned on Pietro Gradenigo, it's quoted in later histories. Whether he said it, and at the time, is unknown.

claims.text: Manin handed his ducal cap to his servant, saying he wouldn't need it any more.
claims.note: The most famous line of the fall, from later accounts. It sums up the day too neatly to be fully trusted.

claims.text: The Great Council voted 512 to 20 to dissolve itself, without a legal quorum.
claims.note: The figures are the commonly given ones. Some sources give slightly different counts, and the quorum point is often debated.
